en: The Later Part of the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll One.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Jñānabhadra of Boliṅg in the Southern Sea during the Great Tang Dynasty.

The Remainder of the Kauṇḍinya Chapter: At that time, Subhadra, having heard from the Buddha the profound and wondrous Dharma of the Great Parinirvāṇa, attained the Dharma-eye and beheld the purity of the Dharma. Cherishing the True Dharma, he abandoned all false views and developed firm and deep faith in the Buddha’s teachings;
he then sought to go forth as a renunciant under the Tathāgata.
The Buddha said:
"Excellent, excellent, Subhadra!"
"Welcome, Bhikṣu! You have pleased the Noble One’s heart and have well entered the Buddha-way.

Thereupon, Subhadra was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; his delight was immeasurable. Immediately, his hair and beard fell away of their own accord, and he became a śramaṇa. The water of the wisdom of the Dharma-nature poured into the source of his mind; he was no longer bound by attachments, his outflows were exhausted, his mind was liberated, and he attained the fruit of Arhatship.

Having realized the fruit, Subhadra approached the Buddha, gazed up at the Honored One’s countenance, and prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet. He bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and joined his palms. With a mixture of sorrow and joy, he deeply repented for his past transgressions and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

I lament that this poisonous body of mine has, throughout the long succession of kalpas, constantly deceived and deluded me, causing me to remain submerged for a long time in ignorance and false views, drowning in the dharmas of the three realms and the paths of externalists—how painful it is!
Alas! The harm has been exceedingly great.
Now, in great joy and celebration, we receive the grace of the Tathāgata and have attained entry into the True Dharma.

The World-Honored One’s ocean of wisdom is vast and his compassion is immeasurable; I humbly reflect that even if I were to sacrifice my body over successive kalpas, I could not repay this brief moment of grace.
Having spoken these words, Subhadra wept with tears streaming down his face, unable to restrain himself, and addressed the Buddha again:
"World-Honored One!
I am advanced in years and my remaining life is but short; I have not yet escaped the manifold sufferings, and the suffering of conditioned existence presses upon me."
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will remain for a short while to provide instruction and admonition; out of compassion, please rescue and protect us, and do not enter parinirvāṇa.
At that time, the World-Honored One remained silent and did not grant his request.
Subhadra, failing to achieve his plea, was filled with grief and distress, and cried out in a loud voice:
"Alas! Alas! The world is empty; the world is empty!"
How is it that now this great terror has arrived and this feverish affliction spreads? Alas! Alas!
"The merit of sentient beings is exhausted, and their eye of true wisdom is extinguished.

Once more he shed tears, wailing with grief and choking with sobs; blood appeared all over his body as he cried out loudly. Before the Tathāgata, he threw his entire body to the ground, his mind becoming frantic and turbid, falling into a state of stupor and unconsciousness.
After a long time, he regained consciousness; with tears streaming down and his voice choked with sobs, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
I cannot bear to see the Tathāgata enter parinirvāṇa; the pain in my heart is so acute that it is beyond my power to restrain."
"How could I possibly dwell together with this fragile vessel of a body, this vessel of poison?
It would be better for me to enter extinction first; I only pray that the World-Honored One will enter parinirvāṇa later."
When Subhadra had spoken these words, he was choked with grief and longing; at that very moment, he entered parinirvāṇa.

Thereupon, unspeakably many, unspeakably many hundreds of millions of *gaṅgā*-sands of great bodhisattvas, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, and all the devas, humans, asuras, and others in the world, cried out with one voice:
"Alas! What suffering!"
"Alas! How is it that the Perfectly Awakened One has suddenly departed? We are now without a master, without a refuge, without support, and without a destination.

Thinking back with longing and affection, they wept with profound grief, grasping one another's hands and beating their breasts. They fainted and lost their sense of direction, their lamentation shaking the trichiliocosm.
At that time, the World-Honored One uttered eight kinds of sounds and addressed the great assembly:
"Do not wail excessively like infants; each of you should exercise self-restraint and do not allow your minds to become disordered."

In this great ocean of birth, death, and the suffering of conditioned existence, you should diligently cultivate a pure mind, never lose mindfulness and wisdom, swiftly seek right knowledge, and quickly emerge from all realms of existence.

The wheel of suffering from assuming bodies within the three realms is boundless; the master of ignorance and the demon-king of affection enslave the body and mind, employing them as servants. As they universally engage with sensory objects, they create the karma of birth and death; greed, anger, and delusion inflict injury at every thought-moment, such that for immeasurable eons one has constantly endured affliction and distress.
What wise person would not reflect upon this source?

You should know that since the distant past, I have already entered great quiescence; I am without aggregates, elements, or sense bases, having forever severed all modes of existence, possessing the diamond-treasury of permanence, bliss, self, and purity.

Now, in this place, I manifest the inconceivable power of skillful means by entering great parinirvāṇa, demonstrating that I am no different from worldly phenomena. I wish to cause sentient beings to know that the body is like a flash of lightning, to give rise to a heart of longing and attachment, and to realize that the torrential river of birth and death flows with such rapidity, and that the revolving of all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) is naturally subject to such a law.
The parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata is profound!
It is most profound!
It is inconceivable!
"This is the realm of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, not something known by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.
The Buddha again addressed the great assembly:
"This Subhadra has already made offerings to Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, having deeply planted roots of goodness in the presence of those Buddhas."

By the power of his original vows, he constantly dwells within the teachings of the Nirgrantha heretics, leaving the household life to practice there; through the wisdom of skillful means, he guides and advances sentient beings who hold false views and have lost the Way, causing them to enter into right knowledge.
Subhadra, by virtue of his original vow, has now encountered me at my final nirvana and been able to hear the True Dharma;
having heard the True Dharma, he has attained the fruit of Arhatship;
and having attained that fruit, he has entered nirvana.
Since I attained the Way and delivered Ājñātakauṇḍinya, until my final nirvāṇa when I delivered Subhadra, my task is complete and there is nothing further to be done;
even if I were to remain for a long time, it would be no different than it is now.
At that time, having spoken these words, the World-Honored One sighed deeply and exclaimed:
"Excellent, excellent!
Subhadra has repaid the Buddha’s kindness; you, the great assembly, should make offerings to his remains and establish a stupa for him."
At that time, the great assembly was filled with sorrow and grief; they suppressed their tears and, following the Buddha’s instructions, cremated his body with fragrant wood, ghee, and oil.
When Subhadra was being cremated, he emitted a great radiance from within the flames and manifested eighteen transformations: water issued from his upper body while fire issued from his lower body;
fire issued from his right side while water issued from his left side;
he manifested as small and then again as large, and manifested as large and then again as small.
It filled the entirety of space.
At that time, an immeasurable multitude of people, as well as various heterodox practitioners and sentient beings with false views, gave rise to the bodhicitta and attained entry into right view.
After Subhadra had manifested these supernatural transformations, he returned once more into the fire.
When the cremation was completed, the great assembly, moved by grief and sorrow, collected the relics and erected a stupa to offer them worship.
1. Chapter on the Bequeathed Teaching, The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Chapter One: The Bequeathed Teaching. At that time, the Buddha addressed Ānanda and the entire great assembly:
"After my parinirvāṇa, you fourfold assembly should diligently protect and uphold my Great Nirvāṇa."

For immeasurable tens of billions of *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, I have cultivated this Great Nirvāṇa Dharma so difficult to attain; it is now fully revealed and explained. You should know that this Great Nirvāṇa is the adamantine jewel-treasury of all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time—eternal, blissful, self, and pure, perfect and without deficiency.
All Buddhas enter parinirvāṇa within this nirvana; it is the ultimate finality, where principle reaches its limit without remainder.
Because all Buddhas here relinquish their bodies and lives, it is called nirvana.
If you wish to attain definitive and true recompense for the Buddha’s kindness;
to swiftly attain Bodhi and receive the crowning touch of all Buddhas upon your heads;
and to never lose right mindfulness throughout every birth in successive lifetimes;
The Buddhas of the ten directions will constantly appear before you and protect you day and night;
they will cause all beings to attain the supramundane Dharma.
You should diligently practice and study this scripture of Nirvana.
The Buddha again addressed Ānanda:

"Before I attained Buddhahood, I manifested entry into the teachings of the non-Buddhist Udraka Rāmaputra, where I practiced and studied the four dhyānas and eight samādhis, receiving and carrying out his instructions."
Since my attainment of Buddhahood, I have disparaged their teachings while gradually leading them forward, until finally Subhadra entered the Buddha-way.
The Tathāgata uses the great torch of wisdom to burn the banners of false views, like throwing dry grass and leaves into a great conflagration.

Ānanda! I am deeply concerned for my kinsmen, the Śākyas. After my parinirvāṇa, you must diligently provide them with excellent instruction and admonition; teach them the sublime Dharma and guide them with a sincere heart. Let them not engage in frivolity, negligence, or distraction, nor enter into various sensory realms to practice false teachings. Before they have escaped the suffering of the triple world, they must seek early deliverance from these five turbidities and the midst of craving and desire.

One should give rise to thoughts of sorrow and fear, and the realization that there is no protection; once this human body is lost, it is difficult to recover. Throughout this single lifetime, one must always remain vigilant, for the great ghost of impermanence seeks its prey and is difficult to escape.
Have compassion for sentient beings and do not kill or harm them, even down to the most minute insects; you should bestow fearlessness upon them.

Purify your physical actions so that you may always be born in a wondrous land; purify your verbal actions so as to remain free from all faults and evils. Do not eat meat and do not drink alcohol; subdue the serpent of the mind and cause it to enter the fruits of the Path.

Reflect deeply upon the retribution for good and evil deeds; they follow one like a shadow follows a form. The cycle of cause and effect across the three periods of existence is never lost; once this life has passed away in vain, there will be no way to undo one's regrets.
"The time for Nirvana has arrived; thus have I shown and taught.

At that moment, having heard the Buddha’s words, Ānanda’s body and mind trembled, his consciousness was overwhelmed with distress, and he choked with suppressed sobs. Deeply submerged in an ocean of grief, his entire being became faint and bewildered; his mind grew dark and turbid as he collapsed before the Tathāgata like one who is dead.
At that time, Aniruddha comforted Ānanda, lightened his sorrowful heart, and said to him:
"Alas! Why do you grieve and suffer?"
"The time for the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa has arrived; though he exists today, he will no longer be here tomorrow morning.
Following my words, inquire of the Tathāgata regarding these four questions:
'After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, how should one dwell with and provide instruction to the group of six bhikṣus who defile families and to the ill-natured Chandaka?'"
"While the Tathāgata is in the world, he takes the Buddha as his teacher; after the World-Honored One has passed away, what shall one take as a teacher?
If while the Buddha is in the world one dwells in reliance upon him, now that the Tathāgata has passed away, in reliance upon what shall one dwell?"
"After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, when the Dharma-piṭaka is compiled, what words should be placed at the beginning of all the sūtras?

At that time, Ānanda was as if emerging from a dream; hearing Aniruddha comfort his heart and prompt him with these four questions, he gradually regained his composure. Overcome with grief beyond measure, he set forth the aforementioned questions in detail and addressed them to the Buddha.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Why do you grieve, suffer, and lament so much?
The transformation of all Buddhas is universal; their deeds are now complete, and the Dharma returns to its ultimate state."
Excellent, excellent, Ānanda!
These four questions you have posed constitute your final inquiry, and they will bring great benefit to all the world.
"Listen attentively, all of you, and reflect upon it well.
"Yes, World-Honored One;
we wish to hear it with joy."
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"Regarding your question as to how one may dwell together with and instruct the six groups of bhikṣus and the ill-natured Chandaka after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, given that they defile the families of others: [it is thus]."
Ānanda! The bhikṣu Chandaka is by nature base and evil; after my parinirvāṇa, he will gradually subdue his mind until it becomes gentle and pliant, and he will abandon his original evil nature.

Ānanda! My younger brother Nanda possessed extremely heavy desire and was by nature base and evil. The Tathāgata, through skillful means, instructed, exhorted, benefited, and gladdened him; having discerned his faculties and nature, he taught him the twelve links of dependent origination by means of the wisdom of *prajñā*.

What are called "ignorance conditions volitional formations, volitional formations condition consciousness," and so on, up to "old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair"—all these are the thicket of ignorance, hatred, and attachment.

All conditioned phenomena are suffering, filling the three realms and flowing throughout the six destinies; this great suffering originates from fundamental ignorance. By means of the wisdom of *prajñā*, one reveals their intrinsic purity; by contemplating the root with clarity, one severs all afflictions and the ignorance of existence.

Because the root is extinguished, ignorance is extinguished; because ignorance is extinguished, volitional formations are extinguished, and so on until old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction are all extinguished.
When one attains this contemplation, the mind is gathered and stabilized, and one immediately enters samādhi.
By the power of samādhi, one enters the first dhyāna, gradually proceeding through the stages until entering the fourth dhyāna, maintaining right mindfulness throughout.
By practicing in this manner, one will subsequently realize the supreme fruit and be liberated from the suffering of the three realms.
Ānanda! At that time, the bhikṣu Nanda gave rise to deep faith and, relying on my teachings, practiced with diligent mind; before long, he attained the fruit of arhatship.

Ānanda! After my parinirvāṇa, you should rely upon my teachings to practice right contemplation and instruct the group of six bhikṣus and Chandaka. If they rely with a profound mind upon this pure, true Dharma, they will before long personally realize the supreme fruit.

“Ānanda! You should know that it is all due to ignorance that the great tree of birth and death within the triple world grows, that one is swept away by the river of craving, that there is the long night of manifold sufferings in darkness, and that one revolves around the pillar of birth and death at the edge of a precipice.

The six consciousnesses are the branches and deluded thoughts are the root; driven by the waves of ignorance within the mind-consciousness, they sport among the six sense objects, sowing the sprouts of suffering and affliction. There is no one able to restrain them, as they act with sovereign freedom like a king.
Therefore I say that ignorance is the master who inflicts injury at every thought-moment; yet sentient beings remain unaware, revolving through birth and death. Ānanda!

All sentient beings, on account of this ignorance, give rise to various fetters of craving. Obscured by the view of self, they are enslaved by eighty-four thousand masters of affliction; their bodies and minds are shattered, and they find no liberation.
Ānanda! If ignorance is extinguished, the three realms are entirely exhausted; for this reason, one is called a world-transcending person. Ānanda!

If one can contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination with clarity, realizing that ultimately there is no self and penetrating deeply into fundamental purity, one will be able to remain far removed from the great fires of the triple world. Ānanda!
The Tathāgata speaks the truth and utters words of sincerity; this is my final entrustment:
you should practice accordingly. Ānanda, as to what you have asked—after the Buddha has passed away, who shall be your teacher?

"Ānanda! The precepts of the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā) are your great teacher; by practicing in reliance upon them, you will be able to attain supramundane, profound concentration and wisdom. Ānanda!"
Regarding your question as to what one relies upon to abide after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa:
Ānanda, one abides by relying on the four foundations of mindfulness to adorn the mind.
To contemplate that the nature and characteristics of the body are identical to empty space is called the application of mindfulness of the body;
to contemplate that sensation is neither internal nor external and does not abide in between is called the application of mindfulness of sensation;
to contemplate that the mind exists only as a name, and that the nature of names is detached [from essence], is called the application of mindfulness of the mind.
To contemplate phenomena without apprehending either wholesome phenomena or unwholesome phenomena is called the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).
Ānanda! All practitioners should dwell in reliance upon these four foundations of mindfulness.
“Ānanda! Regarding what you have asked:
after the Tathāgata has passed into parinirvāṇa, when the Dharma-piṭaka is being compiled, what words should be placed at the beginning of all the sūtras?”
Ānanda! After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, when the Dharma-piṭaka is compiled, you should place at the beginning of all sūtras: “Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was dwelling in such-and-such a region, in such-and-such a place, together with the fourfold assembly, and there he spoke this sūtra.”
At that time, Ānanda again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Whether the Buddha is in the world or after his parinirvāṇa, if a faithful donor should offer gold, silver, the seven treasures, or all manner of articles of pleasure to the Tathāgata, how should these be handled and stored?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"If the Buddha is present, the Saṃgha should know that whatever is offered to the Buddha belongs to the Saṃgha.

But after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, all items offered out of faith to the Buddha should be used to create images of the Buddha, as well as robes for the Buddha, banners and canopies made of the seven precious gems, and to purchase fragrant oils and precious flowers for the purpose of making offerings to the Buddha."
"Except for making offerings to the Buddha, nothing else may be used; whoever uses it commits the offense of stealing the Buddha's property.
Ānanda again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If the Buddha were present, and if there were someone who, with a heart of deep reverence, used gold, silver, the seven treasures, houses, halls, wives, children, slaves, clothing, food and drink, and all manner of articles of pleasure to pay homage and make offerings to the Tathāgata;"

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, if there should be someone who, with gold, silver, the seven treasures, wives and concubines, male and female slaves, clothing, food and drink, and all manner of articles of pleasure, makes offerings to an image of the Tathāgata, honoring it with a profound mind and performing prostrations and worship.
“World-Honored One!
Between these two people who make offerings with such profound resolve, which one obtains the greater merit?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"These two persons, both making offerings with a profound mind, will obtain merit that is no different. Why is this?
Although the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, the Dharma-body remains eternally present; therefore, making offerings with a profound mind results in merit that is exactly equal."
Ānanda again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“If there were someone who, while the Buddha was present, would with a profound mind make offerings and pay homage to the Tathāgata as described above;
and if, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there were another person who, likewise with a profound mind, would make offerings and pay homage to the whole-body śarīra as described above.”
“World-Honored One!
Between these two people, which one would obtain the greater merit?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"These two persons obtain equal merit; their virtue is vast, immeasurable, and boundless, such that even until the end of suffering, their merit shall not be exhausted."
Ānanda again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“If there were someone who, while the Buddha was still present, offered all manner of offerings and paid homage to the Tathāgata with such profound resolve as described above;

and if, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there were another person who, with the same profound resolve, made offerings and paid homage to a half-body relic—[which of these two would generate greater merit?]”
“World-Honored One!
Between these two persons, which one obtains the greater merit?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"These two persons, making offerings with a profound mind, obtain merit that is no different; the merit they acquire is immeasurable and boundless. Ānanda!

If, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there should be someone who, with a profound mind, makes offerings to even a quarter, an eighth, a sixteenth, a hundredth, a thousandth, a ten-thousandth, or a portion as small as a single grain of mustard seed of the Tathāgata’s relics—even down to a fraction the size of a mustard seed—making offerings, honoring, respecting, and praising them all with a profound mind;"
Whether the Buddha is currently present, or if there is another person who, with a profound mind, makes offerings to and reveres the Tathāgata—
these two individuals will obtain equal merit, which is immeasurable and beyond calculation.

Ānanda, you should know that whether the Buddha is present or has entered parinirvāṇa, if there is someone who, with a profound heart, reveres, makes offerings to, prostrates before, honors, and praises him—there is no difference and no distinction between the merit obtained by these two persons.
The Buddha addressed Ānanda and the great assembly:

"After my parinirvāṇa, all sentient beings in the heavens and among humans who obtain my śarīra will experience a mingling of sorrow and joy; moved by grief yet rejoicing in celebration, they shall pay homage, prostrate, and make offerings with a profound mind, thereby attaining immeasurable and boundless merit."
Ānanda! If one sees the relics of the Tathāgata, that is seeing the Buddha; seeing the Buddha is seeing the Dharma; seeing the Dharma is seeing the Saṅgha; and seeing the Saṅgha is seeing Nirvāṇa.
“Ānanda!
You should know that by these causes and conditions, the Three Jewels are eternally abiding, without change, and are able to serve as a place of refuge for sentient beings.
Ānanda again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, by what rules and regulations shall the entire assembly cremate the Tathāgata, obtain his relics, and make offerings to them with a profound mind?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"When I enter parinirvāṇa, you and the great assembly should follow the cremation rites of a Cakravartin King.
Ānanda replied again:
“What are the procedures for the cremation of a Wheel-Turning Sage King? How is it performed?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“After the life of a Wheel-Turning Sage King has ended, his body shall remain for seven days before being placed in an iron coffin.”
Once he had entered the coffin, they immediately filled it to the brim with exquisite fragrant oil and closed the lid so that it was airtight.
After seven more days had passed, he emerged from the coffin, whereupon they bathed and washed him with various scented waters;
having completed the ablutions, they burned a multitude of famous incenses as an offering.

Having first covered his entire body with tūla-cotton, he then wrapped the king’s body all over with a thousand layers of priceless, exquisite white cotton cloth, one placed upon the other in succession.
Once the wrapping was completed, the iron coffin was filled with various fragrant oils, and the body of the Sage King was then placed within it.

Having sealed the coffin tightly, it was carried upon a chariot made of seven precious gems and adorned with fragrant wood. On all four sides of the chariot hung various necklaces and all manner of jeweled cords to embellish it; it was surrounded by offerings of countless flower banners, standards and parasols of the seven precious gems, all kinds of exquisite incense, and all types of celestial music.

Then, using exclusively various exquisite fragrant woods for both the inner and outer casing, they performed the cremation of the body of the Wheel-Turning Sage King with subtle and wondrous fragrant oils.

Once the cremation was completed, they collected the relics and erected a stūpa made of the seven precious gems at a crossroads within the capital city. The stūpa had four gates opened, wherein the relics were enshrined, to be gazed upon by all the world.

“Ānanda! That wheel-turning king succeeded to this royal throne with but meager merit; he was not yet liberated from the realms of existence. He was fully possessed of the five desires, wives, concubines, and court ladies, as well as wrong views, the three poisons, and all afflictions and fetters—not even a hair’s breadth of these had been severed. Yet after his life ended, according to the laws of this world, a stupa was erected for him in worship, and all looked up to it with reverence.”

Ānanda! How much more so for the Tathāgata, who throughout immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable asaṃkhyeya kalpas has forever abandoned the five desires, wives, concubines, and court ladies, and has brought frost and hail upon worldly dharmas.

He is able to exert effort where it is difficult to exert effort, and able to practice what is difficult to practice; he diligently cultivates all the world-transcending ascetic practices of the bodhisattvas.

Regarding the path traversed by all Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time—the profound, subtle, and pure precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, the knowledge and vision of liberation, and the six pāramitās—he is fully endowed with them all.

He has already accomplished and fully perfected all inconceivable merits and wisdom, such as: the ten powers of the Tathāgata, great compassion, the four fearlessnesses, the three gates of liberation, the eighteen kinds of great emptiness, the six supernormal knowledges, the five eyes, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, the thirty-two major marks, the eighty minor characteristics, the lifespans of all Buddhas, all pure Buddha-lands, the maturation of all sentient beings, all difficult ascetic practices, all precepts for gathering virtuous dharmas, all precepts for gathering sentient beings, all precepts for gathering moral discipline, all merits, all wisdom, all adornments, all great vows, and all skillful means. Thus, there is nothing among these that he does not possess in full.

Having severed all that is unwholesome, severed all afflictions, and severed all residual habits of the afflictions; having attained penetration into the Four Noble Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination; having subdued the four māras beneath the Bodhi tree and accomplished the Knowledge of All Modes (sarvajñatā);
and having fully cultivated such sublime dharmas—only then do all Buddhas proclaim: "Excellent!"
"Excellent! Thus, with the water of the wisdom of the Dharma-nature, they were consecrated upon the crown of the Dharmakāya, whereby they attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

For these reasons, I am now titled the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Fully Awakened One of the Ten Directions, the Supreme World-Honored One, peerless among gods and men. I regard all sentient beings equally as I do Rāhula; therefore, I am named Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, and Bhagavat. Out of compassion for the world, having completed my transformative work, I now enter *nirvāṇa* for the sake of sentient beings. Following the ways of the world, I am like a wheel-turning monarch, so that all sentient beings may universally receive offerings.

“Ānanda! When I enter parinirvāṇa, I shall do so like a wheel-turning monarch: after remaining for seven days, I will be placed in an iron coffin, which shall be filled to the brim with exquisite fragrant oil. The lid of the coffin shall be sealed tightly, and its four sides should be adorned with an intermingling of the seven precious jewels. All manner of jeweled banners, incense, and flowers shall be used as offerings.”
After seven days have passed, he shall again emerge from the iron coffin;
having emerged from the coffin, he should wash and bathe the body of the Tathāgata with all kinds of exquisite fragrant waters.

Once washed, he should wrap the entire body with the finest *tūla* cotton, and next, wrap the body of the Tathāgata with one thousand sheets of exquisite, priceless white fine-cloth over the cotton, and then enter the iron coffin once more.

Furthermore, they filled the coffin with exquisite fragrant oils and sealed it tightly. Then, placing the precious coffin upon a chariot adorned with the seven treasures and decorated with every kind of jewel—drawn by pure, exquisite *gośīrṣa* sandalwood, aloeswood, and all manner of fragrant woods—they proceeded to the cremation site. There, countless jeweled banners, countless jeweled canopies, countless jeweled robes, countless celestial music, and countless fragrant flowers completely filled the void as they offered worship with expressions of deep sorrow.

All the devas and humans, along with the countless great assemblies, should each use sandalwood, aloeswood, and exquisite fragrant oils to cremate the Tathāgata, wailing and yearning in sorrowful remembrance.

When the cremation was completed, the assembly of devas and the fourfold community collected the relics and placed them in a vessel of the seven precious gems. Within the capital city, at the crossroads of the four main streets, they erected a stupa made of the seven precious gems to make offerings to the relics; this enabled sentient beings to attain great merit, leave behind the suffering of the three realms of existence, and reach the bliss of Nirvana.
Ānanda, you should know that once the fourfold assembly has erected a stūpa made of the seven precious substances for the Buddha’s relics, they should further erect three other stūpas for veneration:
namely, a stūpa for pratyekabuddhas, a stūpa for arhats, and a stūpa for wheel-turning kings, so that the world may know where to take refuge.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:

“The Tathāgata appears in the world out of compassion for sentient beings, manifesting the ten powers, great compassion, the four fearlessnesses, the twelve links of dependent origination, the Dharma of the four truths, and the three gates of liberation. With an eightfold Brahma-voice that thunders through the three realms and five-colored rays of compassionate light that pervade the six destinies, he accords with the mental karma of sentient beings as it evolves: some attain the fruits of the four stages and the practices of the three vehicles; some realize the untainted and unconditioned path of the pratyekabuddhas; some enter the bodhisattva stages of non-extinction and non-arising; some obtain immeasurable dhāraṇīs; some obtain the five eyes; some obtain the six supernormal powers; some are liberated from the three evil realms; some escape the eight difficulties; and some are freed from the sufferings of the human, celestial, and triple-world realms.”

The Tathāgata’s power of compassion is pure, and the Tathāgata’s dharma-gate of liberation is inconceivable, even unto nirvāṇa. All people of the world, including devas and humans, as well as the fourfold assembly, may erect stupas made of the seven precious jewels to make offerings to the śarīra, thereby attaining great merit; they can cause sentient beings to escape the suffering of the three realms and enter into right liberation.

For these reasons, when the Buddha enters parinirvāṇa, it is only right that the great assemblies of humans and devas throughout all worlds should repay the Buddha’s profound and immeasurable kindness by erecting stūpas made of the seven precious gems to make offerings to his relics; this is indeed how it ought to be.
“World-Honored One!
What benefit do these other three stupas bring to sentient beings, such that they cause them to be erected and to be honored with reverence and offerings?
The Buddha told Ānanda:

“Those Pratyekabuddhas, having awakened to the causal conditions of dharmas and entered into the profound nature of reality, have already been liberated from all the faults and afflictions of existence; they are able to serve as fields of merit for humans and devas. For these reasons, one erects stupas to make offerings to them; the merit thus obtained is second only to that of the Tathāgata, and it can cause all sentient beings to attain sublime fruits.”

Ānanda! As for those Arhats, within the three realms, their karmic destiny for rebirth has been exhausted and they shall not undergo further existence; their holy life is established, and they are able to serve as fields of merit for the world. Therefore, one should erect stupas to make offerings to them; the merit thus obtained is second only to that of a Pratyekabuddha, and it also causes all sentient beings to attain liberation.

Ānanda! Although that wheel-turning king has not yet attained liberation from the afflictions of the three realms, by the power of his merit he governs the four continents and nurtures all living beings through the ten wholesome paths of action. He is thus revered by these sentient beings, and because the fourfold assembly erects stupas to make offerings to him, the merit they obtain is likewise immeasurable.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“When the Buddha enters parinirvāṇa, where among all fourfold assemblies should they cremate the Tathāgata so that his relics may be collected?”
"I only pray that you will grant me instruction.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"When the Buddha enters parinirvāṇa, if all four assemblies perform the cremation of the Tathāgata within the city of Kuśinagara, the people of that city will all succeed to the royal throne; they would then engage in mutual conflict, punishment, and litigation without measure, which would also cause all beings to receive varying degrees of merit."
Ānanda! All four assemblies may perform the cremation of the Tathāgata outside the city,
so that the world may obtain equal merit.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Once the Buddha has entered nirvana and the cremation is completed, and all fourfold assemblies have collected the śarīras and placed them in precious jars, at what location should a stūpa made of the seven treasures be erected so that everyone may make offerings with a profound mind?"
"I only pray that you will grant me instruction. The Buddha told Ānanda:

"After the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa and the cremation is completed, all four assemblies shall collect the śarīra and place them in a jar made of the seven precious substances. Within the city of Kuśinagara, at the intersection of the four main roads, they shall erect a stūpa made of the seven precious substances—thirteen stories high, topped with a *cakra* (wheel-ornament), adorned with an intermixture of all manner of exquisite jewels, and decorated with all kinds of wonderful celestial flowers and banners. The railings on its four sides shall be composed of the seven precious substances; every ornament shall be present without exception. On each of the four sides of the stūpa there shall be one gate, and the windows on each successive level shall be aligned. The jar containing the Tathāgata’s śarīra shall be enshrined therein, so that the devas, humans, and the four assemblies may gaze upon it and make offerings."
Ānanda! The stūpa of a pratyekabuddha should have eleven tiers and should likewise be adorned with various precious gems. Ānanda!
The stūpa of that arhat was completed with four tiers and was likewise adorned with various jewels.
Ānanda! The stūpa of the wheel-turning king was also made of the seven treasures, but it had no further tiers.
"Why is this? Because they have not yet been liberated from the suffering of all existence within the three realms.
At that time, Aniruddha addressed the Buddha, saying:

"After the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa and the cremation has been completed, how shall all the devas, humans, and the fourfold assembly distribute the Tathāgata’s relics so that they may be venerated?"
At that time, the Buddha addressed Aniruddha:

“When I enter parinirvāṇa, you and the devas and humans shall take my śarīra relics and, with an impartial mind, distribute them throughout the three realms and all six destinies for the world to make offerings to.”
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha:
“I now respectfully request from the Buddha half of the Tathāgata’s bodily relics, for it is my deep aspiration to make offerings to them.”
The Buddha told Śakra, Lord of Devas:
“The Tathāgata regards all sentient beings equally, as he does Rāhula; you should not request that half of his relics. Why is this?
"It is for the sake of impartially benefiting and protecting all sentient beings.
The Buddha told Śakra Devendra:
"I now give you one tooth relic from my right upper jaw; you may erect a stūpa in the heavens to make offerings to it, which will enable you to obtain inexhaustible merit and virtue."
At that time, the devas, humans, and the entire great assembly wept with grief, unable to restrain themselves.
Then the World-Honored One addressed the fourfold assembly:
"The Buddha is about to enter parinirvāṇa; you, devas and humans, should not be so deeply distressed."
Why is this? Although the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, his relics remain forever to be venerated.

Furthermore, there is the unsurpassed Dharma Jewel—the Sūtra Piṭaka, the Vinaya Piṭaka, and the Abhidharma Piṭaka. By these causes and conditions, the Triple Gem and the Four Noble Truths abide eternally in the world, enabling sentient beings to take refuge with a profound heart.

Why is this? To make offerings to the śarīra is to make offerings to the Buddha-jewel; to see the Buddha is to see the Dharma-body; to see the Dharma is to see the noble ones (ārya); because one sees the noble ones, one sees the Four Noble Truths; because one sees the Four Noble Truths, one sees Nirvana. Therefore, one should know that the Three Jewels are eternally abiding and subject to no change, for they are able to serve as a refuge for the world.
The Buddha again addressed the great assembly:

"Do not be so deeply distressed. I am now about to enter parinirvāṇa here. If you have any doubts regarding the precepts, the refuges, the permanent or impermanent, the Three Jewels, the Four Noble Truths, the Six Pāramitās, or the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, you should quickly ask questions; let these be your final inquiries."
"After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there will be no further doubt or regret.
He addressed the assembly thus three times.

At that moment, the fourfold assembly was overwhelmed with grief, sorrow, and suffering; they choked back their tears and wept, their hearts pierced by intense pain as they longed for him with deep remembrance. Overcome by the bitterness of their anguish, they were nearly fainting. Yet, through the Buddha's supernatural power, they suppressed their tears and remained silent, with none daring to ask a question.

Why is this? Because all four assemblies have already attained thorough penetration and clear understanding regarding the precepts, the refuges, the Three Jewels, and the Four Noble Truths, and thus possess no doubts.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the fourfold assembly no longer harbored any further doubts, praised them, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
You fourfold assemblies have already attained thorough penetration of the Three Jewels and the Four Noble Truths without doubt, just as pure water washes away the filth from the body."
"You all should apply yourselves with diligent effort to attain liberation early; do not give rise to sorrow, affliction, confusion, or a distracted mind.

At that time, from his lion throne, the World-Honored One used his hand of pure gold to draw aside the saṃghāṭī robe he was wearing, revealing his chest—the color of purple-polished golden lion—displaying it fully to the great assembly, and addressed them, saying:
"All you multitudes of devas and humans, you should, with a profound heart, gaze upon my body, which is the color of purple-polished gold."

At that time, the fourfold assembly all gazed up at the Greatly Awakened World-Honored One’s body, which was the color of pure gold; their eyes did not for a moment turn away, and they were all filled with joy, as if bhikṣus had entered the third dhyāna—a state difficult to give rise to.

At that time, the World-Honored One, having manifested his golden body to the great assembly, immediately emitted immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of rays of light from the Great Parinirvāṇa, universally illuminating all worlds in the ten directions, so that the light of the sun and moon no longer possessed any radiance.
Having emitted this light, he again addressed the great assembly:

"You should know that for your sake, the Tathāgata has undergone diligent toil through successive kalpas, severing his own hands and feet and fully practicing all difficult deeds and ascetic austerities. Through his original vow of great compassion, he has attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* within these five turbidities, obtaining this indestructible, purple-gold vajra-body, complete with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, and immeasurable radiance that universally illumines all things. Those who see his form or encounter his light shall all attain liberation."
The Buddha again addressed the great assembly:
"The appearance of a Buddha in the world is as rare as the udumbara flower; it is extraordinary and difficult to encounter.
You members of this great assembly have met me for the last time; do not let this body pass away in vain."
"By the power of my original vows, I have been born in this defiled land; now that my work of transformation is complete, I wish to enter nirvana.

You should gaze upon my body, which is like purple-polished gold, with a heart of utmost sincerity. You should cultivate such pure karma so that you may attain this fruit and retribution in future ages."
At that time, the World-Honored One repeated this three times, earnestly addressing the great assembly thrice, and revealed his body of pure gold to them.
He then rose from his great lion throne of seven treasures into the air to the height of a *tāla* tree; having ascended, he spoke once more:
"I am about to enter *nirvāṇa*. You, the great assembly, behold my body of purple-golden hue."
In this manner, [the sound] traveled successively to a height of seven *tāla* trees, and for seven times he proclaimed:
"I am about to enter *nirvāṇa*; you, the great assembly, should with deep resolve behold my body, which is the color of purple-polished gold."
Descending from mid-air, he sat upon the lion throne and again addressed the great assembly:
"I am about to enter parinirvāṇa; you should, with deep devotion, behold my body, which is the color of purple-polished gold."
At that time, the World-Honored One rose from his lion throne into the air to the height of one *tāla* tree and again addressed the great assembly:
"I am about to enter parinirvāṇa; you should, with deep resolve, behold my body, which is the color of purple-polished gold."
In this manner, [the light] ascended successively to the height of seven *tāla* trees, and for seven times he addressed them, saying:
"I am about to enter parinirvāṇa; you, the great assembly, behold my body of purple-gold hue."
Descending from mid-air, he sat upon the lion throne and again addressed the great assembly:
"I am about to enter parinirvāṇa; you should, with deep resolve, gaze upon my body, which is the color of purple-polished gold."
At that time, the World-Honored One rose from his lion throne into the air to the height of one tala tree and again addressed the great assembly:
"I am about to enter parinirvāṇa; you should, with deep sincerity, gaze upon my body, which is the color of purple-gold."
In this manner, he rose successively to the height of seven *tāla* trees, and seven times he declared:
"I am about to enter parinirvāṇa; you should gaze with deep devotion upon my body, which is the color of purple-polished gold."
Descending from mid-air and sitting upon the lion throne, he again addressed the great assembly:
"I am about to enter parinirvāṇa; you should, with deep resolve, behold my body, which is the color of purple-polished gold."

At that time, the World-Honored One manifested the Tathāgata’s body, the color of purple-polished gold, displaying it universally to the great assembly. He did this three times, ascending into the air to a height of seven *tāla* trees;
three times he descended from the air and sat upon the lion throne.
Having done so with such earnestness twenty-four times, he addressed the great assembly:

"I am about to enter parinirvāṇa; you should, with deep resolve, behold my vajra-like, firm, and indestructible body of purple-golden hue, which is fearless and as difficult to encounter as the udumbara flower."
"You all should know that I desire to enter nirvana.

You should, with a heart of utmost sincerity, behold my body, which is the color of purple-polished gold, just as a person parched with heat and thirst encounters clear, cool water and drinks until satisfied, having no further thoughts;
you, the great assembly, should do likewise."

I am about to enter parinirvāṇa; you, the great assembly, should gaze upon me with deep devotion, for this is the last time you shall see the Tathāgata. Once you have seen him from this point forward, you shall never behold him again.
"You, the great assembly, have gazed upon me sufficiently; let there be no further regret.
The Buddha again addressed the great assembly:
"After my parinirvāṇa, you, the great assembly, should practice extensively and quickly emerge from the three realms of existence; do not again be indolent, distracted, or negligent."

At that time, all the devas and humans of the four assemblies throughout all worlds who encountered the light of nirvana and gazed upon the Buddha had all their afflictions—whether belonging to the three miserable realms, the eight difficulties, or the world of humans and devas—as well as the four grave offenses, the five heinous crimes, and all other most evil transgressions, forever extinguished without remainder, and they all attained liberation.
At that time, the World-Honored One manifested his body of purple-golden hue, and having earnestly addressed the great assembly, he returned to doning his saṃghāṭī robe as he usually wore it.
Chapter Two: On Returning to the Source. The Buddha again addressed the great assembly:
"The time has now come for me; my entire body is in pain."
Having spoken these words, he immediately entered the first dhyāna and, with the light of nirvāṇa, surveyed the world in its entirety before entering the samādhi of cessation.

At that time, before the World-Honored One had finished speaking, he entered the first dhyāna; from the first dhyāna he emerged and entered the second dhyāna; from the second dhyāna he emerged and entered the third dhyāna; from the third dhyāna he emerged and entered the fourth dhyāna; from the fourth dhyāna he emerged and entered the sphere of infinite space; from the sphere of infinite space he emerged and entered the sphere of infinite consciousness; from the sphere of infinite consciousness he emerged and entered the sphere of nothingness; from the sphere of nothingness he emerged and entered the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; and from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception he emerged and entered the samādhi of cessation.

Emerging from the attainment of cessation, he enters the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; emerging from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he enters the sphere of nothingness; emerging from the sphere of nothingness, he enters the sphere of infinite consciousness; emerging from the sphere of infinite consciousness, he enters the sphere of infinite space; emerging from the sphere of infinite space, he enters the fourth dhyāna; emerging from the fourth dhyāna, he enters the third dhyāna; emerging from the third dhyāna, he enters the second dhyāna; and emerging from the second dhyāna, he enters the first dhyāna.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had thus entered the various dhyānas both in forward and reverse order, he addressed the great assembly:

"With the profound Prajñā, I have universally observed all the three realms and the six destinies, the mountains, the great oceans, and all living beings upon the vast earth. These three realms are fundamentally devoid of intrinsic nature; they are ultimately quiescent and identical in character to empty space."
Without name and without consciousness, one forever severs all modes of existence; fundamentally equal, there is no notion of high or low.
Without seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing, one cannot be bound and cannot be liberated.
There are no sentient beings and no life-span; there is no arising, no originating, no exhaustion, and no cessation.
It is neither the world nor non-world; both nirvana and birth-and-death are unattainable, for the two limits are equal.
Because all phenomena are equal, one dwells in seclusion and tranquility without performing any action; ultimately, even the act of establishing [this state] is unattainable.
From the dharma of non-abiding, the functioning of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) cuts off all marks, such that nothing whatsoever exists.
Such are the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*); those who know this are called world-transcenders.
Not knowing these matters is called the beginning of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).
You, the great assembly, should sever ignorance and extinguish the beginning of birth-and-death.

At that time, having spoken these words, the World-Honored One again entered the transcendental dhyānas: he emerged from the first dhyāna and entered the third dhyāna; from the third dhyāna he emerged and entered the sphere of infinite space; from the sphere of infinite space he emerged and entered the sphere of nothingness; from the sphere of nothingness he emerged and entered the meditative attainment of cessation.

Emerging from the meditative attainment of cessation, he returned in succession until he reached the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception he emerged and entered the sphere of infinite consciousness; from the sphere of infinite consciousness he emerged and entered the fourth dhyāna; from the fourth dhyāna he emerged and entered the second dhyāna; and from the second dhyāna he emerged and entered the first dhyāna.
Having thus entered the meditative absorptions (dhyāna) in both reverse and direct order and by leaping over them, he again addressed the great assembly:

"With the Mahāprajñā, I have universally observed all sentient and non-sentient beings within the triple world, as well as all persons and phenomena; they are all ultimately such that there is neither one who is bound nor one who is liberated."
Without a master and without reliance, it cannot be grasped or maintained.
It does not emerge from the three realms, nor does it enter into the various states of existence.

Primordially pure, stainless, and free from afflictions, it is equal to space; it is neither unequal nor non-unequal. When all stirring thoughts are exhausted and the conceptualizing mind ceases, such a characteristic of phenomena is called Great Nirvana.
"To truly see this Dharma is called liberation; that ordinary people do not know it is called ignorance.

Having spoken these words, he again entered the meditative absorptions beyond [the four dhyānas], emerging from the first dhyāna and entering the attainment of cessation, and emerging from the attainment of cessation and entering the first dhyāna.
Having thus entered the meditative absorptions (dhyāna) in both reverse and direct order and by leaping over them, he again addressed the great assembly:

"I have observed all phenomena throughout the triple world with the Buddha-eye; the fundamental limit of ignorance is by nature originally liberated. Even if one were to seek it throughout the ten directions, it could not be found, for since its root does not exist, its causes, branches, and leaves are all entirely liberated."
Because of liberation from ignorance, there is liberation even unto old age and death.
For this reason, I now abide in the light of eternal quiescence, which is called Great Nirvana.

At that time, Ānanda was overcome with boundless sorrow, grief, anguish, and mental derangement; his consciousness was so clouded that he was like one heavily intoxicated, entirely devoid of awareness. He did not see the fourfold assembly, nor did he know whether the Tathāgata had already entered parinirvāṇa or had not yet done so.

At that time, the World-Honored One thus three times entered various meditative absorptions from the state of transcendence to universally observe the Dharma-realm, preaching the Dharma thrice for the great assembly; in this manner, the Tathāgata proceeded through twenty-seven successive cycles, entering various meditative absorptions.
Because Ānanda did not know, as soon as the Buddha entered the first dhyāna, he would pose a question; this occurred twenty-seven times in succession, and he asked Aniruddha:
"Has the Buddha already entered parinirvāṇa, or has he not yet entered it?"
Aniruddha, deeply knowing that the Tathāgata had entered various meditative absorptions, answered Ānanda twenty-seven times:
"The Buddha has not yet entered parinirvāṇa.
At that time, the entire great assembly was utterly bewildered, unable to discern whether the Tathāgata had entered parinirvāṇa or not.

At that time, the World-Honored One entered various meditative concentrations three times and instructed the assembly three times. Having done so, he lay down on his right side upon a bed of seven treasures, with his head toward the north, his feet toward the south, his face toward the west, and his back toward the east. That bed of seven treasures was adorned with exquisite necklaces and ornaments. In the śāla grove stood four pairs of trees—eight in total: one pair to the west in front of the Tathāgata, one pair to the east behind the Tathāgata, one pair to the north at the Buddha’s head, and one pair to the south at the Buddha’s feet.
At that time, the World-Honored One was reclining upon a jeweled couch beneath a śāla grove; at the middle of the night, he entered the fourth dhyāna, remaining silent and still.
At that very moment, he entered parinirvāṇa.

After the Greatly Awakened World-Honored One had entered parinirvāṇa, the two pairs of śāla trees to the east and west merged into a single tree, and the two pairs to the north and south likewise merged into a single tree. These trees hung down and covered the jeweled couch, sheltering the Tathāgata; yet immediately, they turned a dismal white like white cranes. Their branches, leaves, flowers, fruits, bark, and trunks all split and fell away, gradually withering and decaying until nothing remained but broken fragments.

At that time, the entire great earth throughout the countless hundreds of thousands of billions of *Ganges-sand* Buddha-worlds in the ten directions shook violently, and various sounds issued forth, crying out:
"Alas! What suffering!"
"Alas! The world is empty and void," he cried out,
uttering sounds of lamentation for impermanence, suffering, and emptiness.

At that time, all the mountains in the worlds of the ten directions—the Mount Mucilinda, the Mount Mahāmucilinda, the Cakravāḍa Mountains, the Mahācakravāḍa Mountains, all the Sumeru Mountains, the Fragrant Mountains, the Jewel Mountains, the Gold Mountains, the Black Mountains, and every mountain upon the entire great earth—simultaneously quaked and split asunder; they all collapsed and fell, emitting a great sound that roared through the worlds, crying out:
"Alas! How bitter!"
Alas! How is it that in a single moment the world has been left orphaned and exposed? The Sun of Wisdom has set behind the mountain of Great Nirvana;
all sentient beings have lost their true father of compassion and their revered deity, leaving them with no one to look up to.
At that time, all the great oceans throughout the worlds of the ten directions became turbid and churned with surging waves, emitting various sounds that cried out:
"Alas! What suffering!"

Alas! The Perfectly Awakened One has already passed into extinction; sentient beings, burdened by the suffering of their transgressions, shall long wander through the great ocean of birth and death for many nights. Having lost their way on the correct path, by what means can they attain liberation?
At that time, all rivers, streams, ravines, gullies, torrents, springs, canals, wells, and bathing pools were completely overturned, their waters entirely dried up and exhausted.

At that time, throughout the worlds of the ten directions, the great earth and the void became still and profoundly dark; the brilliant light of the sun and moon ceased to shine entirely, and a gloom of darkness and sorrow pervaded the world.
At that moment, a sudden black wind arose, raging and shaking with such force that it blew sand and dust until the world was shrouded in darkness.
At that time, all the grasses, trees, medicinal herbs, flowers, fruits, branches, and leaves upon the great earth were utterly broken and crushed, falling away without exception.
At that moment, all the devas of the worlds in the ten directions filled the void, wailing and lamenting so as to shake the trichiliocosm.

They rained down countless hundreds of thousands of various kinds of exquisite celestial incense and heavenly flowers, filling the trichiliocosm and rising high like Mount Sumeru as an offering to the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, from the sky above, they rained down countless celestial banners, pennants, necklaces, canopies, and precious jewels, which filled the void and transformed into jeweled terraces. With pearl necklaces and strings of the seven treasures draped on all four sides, their radiant splendor served as an offering to the Tathāgata.
In the sky above, countless subtle celestial music was again performed; drums, pipes, strings, and songs produced all manner of sounds, proclaiming:
"Alas! How bitter!"

Alas! The Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa; the world is desolate and void. The eye of sentient beings has been extinguished, and the rākṣasa of afflictions and great desire circulate freely. The continuity of the suffering of conditioned existence persists, and the wheel of pain turns without ceasing.
At that time, Ānanda was so overwhelmed by panic and confusion that he lost all awareness; he did not know whether the Tathāgata had already entered parinirvāṇa or had not yet entered it.
Seeing only an extraordinary and unprecedented sight, he again asked Loutou,
"Has the Buddha entered nirvana?
Loutou replied:
“The Greatly Awakened World-Honored One has already entered parinirvāṇa.
When Ānanda heard these words, he fainted and fell to the ground like a dead man; silent and breathless, he was in a state of profound darkness and unconsciousness.
At that time, Rudrāyaṇa sprinkled clear, cool water on Ānanda’s face, supported him to help him rise, and comforted him with skillful means, saying to Ānanda:
"How tragic!"
Alas! What suffering! What can be done? What can be done!
Do not let your minds be disturbed by great sorrow, poison, or the heat of affliction.
The Tathāgata’s work of transformation is complete; no one among the humans or devas can detain him.
Alas! How bitter it is!
Alas! What can be done? What can be done?
Who would have expected that today the Teacher of Gods and Humans would reach the end of his task, with none able to detain him?
How tragic! Let us, you and I, together restrain our grief for a while.
He further consoled him, saying: "Ānanda!
Although the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, his relics and the unsurpassed Dharma-treasure remain forever in the world, able to serve as a refuge for sentient beings."

"I and you all should apply ourselves with diligent vigor to bestow the jewel of the Buddha-dharma upon sentient beings, enabling them to be liberated from all sufferings and to repay the grace of the Tathāgata.
At that time, having heard these words of consolation, Ānanda gradually regained his composure; yet he choked with emotion and shed tears, overcome by grief beyond measure.

In the Śāla grove at the city of Kuśinagara, spanning thirty-two yojanas in length and breadth, the great assembly of devas and humans completely filled it; even the tip of a sharp needle could accommodate immeasurable multitudes, with no gaps between them and without any mutual obstruction.

At that time, countless billions of bodhisattvas and the entire great assembly were all bewildered and distressed; their minds became clouded and turbid, and they could not perceive at all whether the Tathāgata had entered parinirvāṇa or had not yet entered parinirvāṇa.
Seeing only constant change and flux, they all simultaneously asked Loutou,
"Has the Buddha entered nirvana?
At that time, Loutou addressed the great assembly of all devas and humans:
“The Greatly Awakened World-Honored One has already entered *nirvāṇa*.

At that time, having heard these words, the countless members of the great assembly were all simultaneously overcome by confusion and fainting, collapsing to the ground. Bitter anguish entered their hearts; their throats were choked so they could not utter a sound. Among them, some followed the Buddha into extinction, some lost consciousness, some trembled with both body and mind, some grasped one another’s hands while sobbing and shedding tears, some constantly beat their breasts and cried out loudly, some raised their hands to strike their heads and pluck out their hair, and some cried out:
“Alas! How painful!”
"How painful!
How bitter and poisonous is this suffering!"— thus some cried out.
"How swift is the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa! Some cried out,
"We have lost our revered deity," while others lamented:
Regarding the statement, "The world is empty and the eyes of sentient beings have perished," some lamented, saying, "The great demons of affliction have already spread abroad";
others lamented, saying, "The seeds and sprouts of the goodness of sentient beings have perished"; and still others lamented, saying:

Regarding the phrase "The Māra King joyfully cast off his armor": some rebuked themselves for contemplating the impermanence of body and mind; some attained liberation through correct contemplation; some lamented their lack of refuge; and among them, some had blood appear all over their bodies, which flowed and drenched the ground. With such diverse forms and distinct voices, the mournful cries of the entire assembly reverberated throughout all worlds.

At that time, Śikhin, the Great Brahmā King and Lord of the Sahā World, knowing that the Buddha had already entered nirvana, together with the hosts of devas, descended through the air from the First Dhyāna. Raising their voices in loud lamentation, they wept and choked with grief; they threw themselves before the Tathāgata, fainted and fell to the ground, and only after a long time regained consciousness.
Overcome by sorrow beyond measure, they immediately uttered these verses of mournful praise before the Buddha:
“The World-Honored One’s original vow of old Was to dwell in this Land of Endurance for our sake.”
He conceals his immeasurable power of mastery, employing the Dharma that the poor delight in to deliver sentient beings.
Through skillful means, he teaches according to what is appropriate and responsive; there are none among sentient beings who do not receive peace and happiness.
He guides and encourages them to escape the suffering of the three realms of existence, so that ultimately all reach the path of Nirvana.
The Tathāgata, like a compassionate mother, nurtured all sentient beings; He universally nourished them with the milk of great compassion.
How could one have expected that he would suddenly abandon us in an instant, Leaving gods and humans orphaned and exposed, with no place of refuge?
Alas! The sprouts of the seeds of goodness in sentient beings lack the celestial nectar to cause them to grow;
once these wholesome sprouts have gradually withered away, they are dragged by their own sinful karma into the evil realms.
Alas! The world is entirely empty and void; the true eye of wisdom in sentient beings has already perished.
Having walked within the darkness of ignorance, they fall into the three realms of existence and drown in suffering.
Alas, sentient beings have no savior for their sins; may they attain liberation by relying on the śarīra.
We entreat the Tathāgata’s power of great compassion to rescue and protect us, so that we may escape this ground of suffering.
"How painful is this evil world, that the Tathāgata abandons us and enters nirvāṇa!
At that time, Śakra Devendra and the great assembly descended from the sky, crying out:
"Alas! How bitter!"
"Alas! How bitter!
he cried out, weeping bitterly with tears streaming down his face. He threw himself before the Tathāgata, fell to the ground in a swoon, and only after a long time regained consciousness.
With a voice choked by grief, he knelt on his right knee before the Buddha and uttered these verses in lamentation:
"The Tathāgata practiced austerities throughout kalpas, Universally for the sake of us, the multitude of sentient beings;
Having attained the path of unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, He nurtures all beings equally, as if they were his only child."
Among those who bestow the medicine of Dharma, you are the supreme medicine; among physicians who treat illness, you are the most excellent physician.
With great clouds of compassion, you shelter all sentient beings, raining down the nectar of wisdom upon everything.
The light of the sun of wisdom illuminates the darkness of ignorance; sentient beings in ignorance behold the Noble Path.
The compassionate light of the moon of the Sage shines upon the six realms of existence; those within the three worlds receive its light and are liberated from all suffering.
How could it be that you now abandon great compassion?
Having entered nirvana, the multitude no longer sees you.
Where now is the great compassion of your original vow?
Abandoning sentient beings like mucus or spittle, all of us sentient beings will surely die like a calf that has lost its mother.
The fourfold assembly, holding one another’s hands, weeps; beating their breasts in great lamentation, they move the three realms.
Alas, alas, all you people! How is it that in a single day you have all been left orphaned and exposed?
Our merit is exhausted; how extreme is our suffering!
The sprouts of goodness are scorched and withered, no longer moistened by dew.
I only pray that the light of the Dharma-treasure and the śarīra relics Shall illuminate me and cause me to escape the suffering of the three realms of existence.
Alas! How painful it is for us, this multitude; When shall we again behold the Tathāgata?
At that time, Rāhula wept with sorrow and lamented boundlessly; kneeling before the Buddha, he praised him with these verses of grief:
“The Dharma-King of Perfect Enlightenment has nurtured us, Feeding us the milk of the Dharma to grow our Dharma-bodies.
Yet the Dharma-bodies of sentient beings are not yet established, And their lives of wisdom lack sufficient provisions.”
One should constantly expound the Dharma with the eightfold voice, so that all who hear it may fully awaken to the Way;
one should constantly radiate the five-colored light of great compassion, so that all who receive this light may attain liberation.
How can you enter eternal nirvana today?
Upon what shall suffering beings rely? Alas!
If the World-Honored One abandons his great compassion, we, left orphaned and destitute, shall surely die.
Although we know that the World-Honored One manifests skillful means, none among us are able to refrain from sorrow.
The fourfold assembly is bewildered and fainting, their minds darkened and lost; their lamentation moves heaven and earth and shakes the three realms.
While the World-Honored One dwells alone in great peace and bliss, where shall sentient beings go amidst their great suffering?
In the past, for our sake, the World-Honored One, throughout many kalpas, gave up his head and severed his hands and feet;
having attained the path of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, he will not remain long in the world but shall enter parinirvāṇa.
I and the fourfold assembly dwell in ignorance; the King of Māras rejoices and casts off his armor.
Alas, World-Honored One, we pray for your great compassion; may the compassionate light of your relics gather us in.
We humbly entreat the World-Honored One to have pity on the fourfold assembly; may the flow of the Dharma-treasure be inexhaustible.
We cannot bring ourselves to perish this very moment; yet if we merely preserve our remaining lives, how much longer can they last?
Alas! This pain is so piercing it is unbearable; to behold the World-Honored One once more seems beyond all hope.

At that time, Ānanda fainted and then gradually regained consciousness; he raised his hands to strike his head, beat his chest, and choked with sobs. Weeping bitterly with tears streaming down, overcome by grief beyond measure, he knelt long before the Buddha and lamented in verse:
"By the power of my former vow with the Buddha, I was fortunate enough to be born together with him among the Śākyas.
Since the Tathāgata attained the path of Perfect Enlightenment, I have served as his attendant for twenty years."
With a profound heart, my reverence and offerings were never enough; yet in a single day, you have abandoned me to enter nirvana.
How painful!
How lamentable!
The bitter poison of suffering brings agonizing pain to the heart throughout the infinite long night.
My body has not yet escaped the net of existence, nor have I emerged from the shell of ignorance;
the beak of the World-Honored One’s wisdom has not yet pecked it open—how can you abandon me and enter parinirvāṇa so soon?
I am like a newborn infant; having lost my mother, I shall surely die before long.
World-Honored One, why do you abandon me, so that I must wander alone within the triple world while you enjoy peace and bliss?

I now repent before the World-Honored One: having served the Buddha for twenty years, I have been frequently indolent and lax in my four modes of deportment, unable to please the heart of the Great Sage.
May the World-Honored One of Perfect Enlightenment, out of great compassion, bestow upon me the nectar of immortality and grant me peace and happiness;
may I, throughout the exhaustion of the future eons, always behold the World-Honored One and serve as his attendant.
I only pray that the World-Honored One’s light of great compassion will embrace me throughout all worlds.
Alas, alas! It is beyond words!
Choking with sobs, how can I possibly express the Sage’s grace?

At that time, countless billions of bodhisattvas—equal in number to the sands of the Ganges—as well as the entire assembly of gods and humans in the world, took one another’s hands, weeping with tears streaming down their faces; overcome by grief, they could not restrain themselves, yet each tried to suppress their sorrow for the sake of the others.

Thereupon, they each prepared countless exquisite fragrant flowers—*māndārava*, *mahāmāndārava*, *mañjūṣaka*, and *mahāmañjūṣaka* flowers—as well as countless celestial and terrestrial *candana* and aloeswood from the seashores, hundreds of thousands of kinds of blended incenses, countless fragrant pastes, scented waters, precious canopies, jeweled banners, precious pennants, pearls, and necklaces. These filled the entirety of space; they cast them before the Tathāgata and made offerings with deep sorrow.

At that time, all the people within the city of Kuśinagara—men and women, old and young—were filled with grief and shed tears. Each prepared countless exquisite fragrant flowers, banners, canopies, and other offerings, even more magnificent than before, and went to where the Tathāgata was to pay him homage with sorrowful devotion.

At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings and the assembly of devas wept with sorrowful tears; each prepared countless fragrant flowers and all manner of offerings, three times more than before. Weeping and shedding tears, they came to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves before the Tathāgata, and made offerings with deep grief.
The gods of the five heavens were thus twice as superior as those before;
the same was true for the gods of the form realm and the formless realm, who offered twice as superior worship.
