Chapter Three: The Miraculous Response at the Cremation At that time, all the men and women within the city of Kuśinagara wept with flowing tears, not knowing the ritual procedures for the cremation. They asked Ānanda, saying:
"Now that the Tathāgata has entered nirvāṇa, what ritual procedures should be followed for his cremation?"
At that time, Śakra recounted the aforementioned matters in detail and replied, "As the Buddha has taught, one should rely upon the Dharma of the Wheel-Turning King.

Then, all the people within the city of Kuśinagara wept with flowing tears and entered the city together. They immediately fashioned a golden coffin adorned with the seven treasures, prepared one thousand sheets of exquisite, priceless white cotton cloth, and countless fine, soft, and wonderful *tūla* cottons. They also prepared countless exquisite sandalwood and aloeswood, hundreds of thousands of kinds of blended incenses, fragrant mud, and scented water, as well as all manner of silk canopies, banners, and flowers; these filled the sky like clouds, heaped up as high as Mount Sumeru.

Having completed the preparations, he shed tears of sorrow and led [the relics] to the Buddha’s dwelling; prostrating himself before the Tathāgata, overcome with grief and sobbing, he offered his worship.

At that time, all the people within the city of Kuśinagara and the great multitude were once again overcome with grief; their voices choked with sobs and tears flowing down, they further brought immeasurable incense, flowers, banners, canopies, and all manner of offerings, which filled the sky like clouds. Holding hands and beating their breasts, they choked with emotion as tears filled their eyes; their lamentation shook the great trichiliocosm as they cast themselves before the Tathāgata to make offerings in sorrowful devotion.

At that time, the great assembly, choked with sobs and deep with reverence, each used fine, exquisite white cotton cloth to cover their hands as they assisted the Tathāgata into the golden coffin; they filled it to the brim with fragrant oil, and the coffin doors were then closed.

At that time, all the men and women within the city of Kuśinagara, desiring merit and with hearts full of goodness, wished to take possession of the Tathāgata’s virtues so that the entire assembly of devas and humans would not lift the Buddha’s coffin together. They immediately consulted one another and dispatched four Malla warriors, peerless in their great strength, who stripped off the necklaces, garments, and ornaments they were wearing, vowing in their hearts to lift the holy coffin of the Tathāgata as they entered the city to personally present their offerings; yet, even though they exerted all their supernatural power, they could not prevail.

At that time, eight more powerful mahānagna wrestlers were dispatched from within the city to the place where the holy coffin was located; they stripped off their garments and together lifted the Buddha’s coffin, yet they could not move it at all, despite exhausting all their supernatural strength.

Within the city of Kuśinagara, sixteen more extremely powerful wrestlers were dispatched to the location of the coffin; they removed their garments and together attempted to lift the Buddha’s coffin, yet they were likewise unable to move it.
At that time, Rudrāyaṇa said to the Mallas:
"Even if all the people within the city—men and women, great and small—were to lift the Tathāgata’s coffin together to bring it into the city, they would still not be able to do so."
"How much less could you possibly prevail?
You must request the great assembly and the power of all the devas to assist you in lifting the coffin; only then shall it enter the city.

Before Loutou had finished speaking, Śakra-devānām-indra immediately took up a sublime great canopy of the seven precious gems, along with countless fragrant flowers, banners, streamers, and music. Accompanied by the host of devas, weeping and shedding tears, he suspended them in mid-air to make offerings to the holy coffin.
Reaching as far as the sixth heaven and the heavens of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), all offered worship to the holy coffin just as Śakra had done.
At that time, the World-Honored One’s great compassion universally covered all, causing all beings in the world to attain a mind of equanimity and receive blessings without distinction.

In the Śāla grove, he himself lifted the coffin and ascended into the air to a height of one *tāla* tree; neither all the people within the city of Kuśinagara nor the great assembly of worldly humans, devas, and others were able to lift the holy coffin of the Buddha.

At that time, Śakra and the host of devas took up a great canopy of the seven treasures and a jeweled pavilion with four pillars, adorned on all four sides with necklaces of the seven treasures; they suspended these in mid-air to cover the holy coffin of the Buddha. With countless fragrant flowers, banners, streamers, necklaces, music, and exquisite multicolored fabrics, they made offerings in the sky.

Upon reaching the sixth heaven, the realm of the Yāma-devas, the devas there doubled their previous offerings to the holy coffin of the Buddha and extended their worship even further than Śakra had done.
At that time, all the people within the city of Kuśinagara, seeing the holy coffin of the Buddha ascend into the air, beat their breasts and wailed loudly, sobbing in grief and distress.

At that time, all the devas and humans, before the precious coffin of the Great Holy One, scattered everywhere seven kinds of jewels, pearls, fragrant flowers, necklaces, and exquisite multicolored silks; they fell in profusion like clouds, completely filling both the earth and the void. Weeping with sorrow and shedding tears, they made offerings to the Tathāgata’s miraculous coffin of seven jewels, crying out in unison:
"Alas! How bitter!"
"Alas! We are devoid of merit;
we have lifted the holy coffin of the Buddha but are unable to move it. We are orphaned and destitute; what roots of goodness could we possibly possess?
At that time, the World-Honored One’s great and holy golden coffin, amidst the void of the Śāla grove, slowly ascended into the air and entered through the western gate of Kuśinagara.

At that time, all the men and women within the city of Kuśinagara, along with countless bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and the great assembly of devas and humans, filled both the earth and the void. Following the sublime and sacred coffin of the Tathāgata, they held one another’s hands, wailing and weeping aloud, beating their breasts and crying out, sobbing and shedding tears. Each carried countless fragrant flowers, precious banners, and canopies, filling both the earth and the void; they lamented and sighed in sorrow, making offerings to the sacred coffin.

On one side of the city of Kuśinagara, the area measured forty-eight *yojanas* in length and breadth. At that time, the Tathāgata’s golden coffin made of the seven precious gems slowly ascended into the air; it emerged from the eastern gate of Kuśinagara, traveled through the air to the right, and entered the southern gate. Proceeding gradually through the air, it exited the northern gate, ascended into the air to the left, and returned to enter through the western gate of Kuśinagara.

Having thus circled three times in succession, it again ascended slowly into the air and entered the western gate; traveling through the air, it exited the eastern gate, proceeded through the air to the left, and entered the northern gate of the city. Traveling gradually through the air, it exited the southern gate, ascended into the air to the right, and returned to enter the western gate. Thus, it continued to circle in succession until it had completed four circuits.
Thus, they circumambulated the city of Kuśinagara seven times to the left and right.

At that time, as the holy coffin made of the seven treasures was entering the city, the entire great assembly wailed with grief and choked with sobs. Each person brought countless exquisite fragrant woods—sandalwood, aloeswood, and all kinds of precious incense—with grain-like patterns and pure fragrance that perfumed the entire world.
Furthermore, they carried countless jeweled banners, canopies, flowers, and necklaces to the site of the cremation, making offerings with profound sorrow.

At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings and the assembly of devas wept with flowing tears; each held five hundred pieces of the most exquisite celestial sandalwood and aloeswood—pure both inside and out, their fragrance pervading everywhere—each as large as a chariot wheel.
Furthermore, they brought all manner of precious incense, jeweled banners, jeweled canopies, wonderful flowers, and necklaces to the site of the cremation, making offerings with deep sorrow.

The devas of the Second Heaven each brought one thousand pieces, those of the Third Heaven two thousand, the Fourth Heaven three thousand, the Fifth Heaven four thousand, and the Sixth Heaven five thousand, along with streamers and flowers, arriving at the site of the cremation to make offerings with grief.
At that time, the devas of the form realm and the formless realm brought only fragrant flowers to the site of the cremation, where they made offerings with deep sorrow.

At that time, the great assemblies of all the world, each carrying exquisite sandalwood, aloeswood, fragrant flowers, banners, and canopies, went to the site of the cremation, where they made offerings with deep sorrow.

At that time, Loutou’s eyes were filled with tears and his grief was boundless. He entreated the devas and humans for exquisite fragrant wood—sandalwood and aloeswood—amounting to six thousand pieces, with grainy textures and pure fragrance that spread in all directions. Arriving at the site of the cremation, he made offerings with profound sorrow.
The Lake Anavatapta is two hundred yojanas in length and breadth on all four sides, from which four great rivers flow.

When the Buddha first attained enlightenment, on the northern bank of the Ganges River, a single sandalwood tree sprang up following the Buddha; it was as large as a chariot wheel and seven *tāla* trees in height, its fragrance wafting everywhere as an offering to the Tathāgata.
The deity of that fragrant tree was born together with the tree; she constantly took this incense to make offerings to the Buddha.
When the Buddha entered nirvana, this single sandalwood tree perished along with him: its bark and leaves fell away, and the deity also died with it.
Various other deities took this fragrant tree and conveyed it to the site of the cremation, where they made offerings with deep sorrow.

That ground is the place where all Buddhas of the three periods of time have been cremated; by the power of his original vows, the Greatly Awakened World-Honored One likewise underwent cremation at this very spot.
In this place are the immeasurable jewel stupas of the Buddhas of antiquity, a site of indestructible diamond-like solidity.

At that time, the Great Sage Tathāgata’s precious coffin gradually traveled through the air to the site of the cremation; it slowly descended from the sky and was placed upon a bed of the seven jewels, which was adorned with all manner of exquisite necklaces and priceless multicolored silks.

At that time, after another seven days had passed, all the men and women within the city of Kuśinagara, along with countless bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and the entire assembly of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, followed the Buddha’s coffin for seven days with weeping and choked voices, carrying various banners, canopies, precious standards, incense, and flowers. By the Buddha’s supernatural power, none of the devas or humans felt hunger or thirst; not one of them thought of food, but they saw only their sorrowful weeping and their longing devotion to the Tathāgata.
When the seven days had passed, the Great Sage, the Tathāgata, was about to emerge from his coffin.

At that time, all the men and women within the city of Kuśinagara, along with a vast multitude, wept again with great sorrow, causing the world to tremble. They further brought fragrant flowers, countless banners and canopies, and exquisite celestial music, placing them before the Buddha’s coffin and making offerings while wailing in grief.

At that time, the great assembly choked with grief and shed tears; each used fine white cotton cloth to cover their hands, and with profound reverence, they supported the Tathāgata’s body—of purple-gold hue, adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, a firm and indestructible diamond-like form—from the precious coffin. He emerged calmly and was placed upon a bed of the seven treasures.

At that time, the great assembly was overcome with profound sorrow, their voices shaking the worlds of all Buddhas throughout the ten directions. Furthermore, they offered deep-seated devotion through all manner of incense, flowers, silken canopies, and music; fainting and sobbing, they threw themselves before the Tathāgata.

At that time, the great assembly again wept with deep sorrow, their eyes overflowing with tears. Each took countless perfumed waters and fragrant muds, and with profound and reverent hearts, they washed from head to foot the Tathāgata’s indestructible body—adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, the infinite merit and wisdom of vajra-like solidity, and the lustrous hue of purple-polished gold. They further washed the precious coffin until it was exquisitely pure.

Once the ablution was completed, the great assembly again wailed and wept bitterly, their voices choked with grief. They burned exquisite incense and scattered flowers of the seven precious gems; countless jeweled banners, streamers, and canopies filled both the earth and the void as they lamented and cried out in sorrow, making offerings to the Tathāgata.

At that time, the great assembly was filled with grief and choked with sobs; they immediately took countless fine *tūla* cottons and wrapped them from head to foot around the Tathāgata’s adamantine-colored body.
Once the body was thus wrapped, they further wound the Tathāgata’s body with a thousand layers of exquisite, priceless white cotton cloth, each layer placed one upon another over the *tūla* cotton.

When the wrapping was complete, the great assembly was overcome with profound sorrow; they wailed and wept until they fainted, and once again offered worship with choked voices, presenting incense, flowers, banners, canopies, jeweled standards, and music.

At that time, the great assembly wept with flowing tears; with hearts of profound and heavy reverence, each used white cotton cloth to cover their hands, sobbing and choked with grief as they together assisted the Tathāgata into the precious coffin. They filled it to the brim with fragrant oil, and the coffin doors were immediately closed.

At that time, the great assembly was overcome with profound sorrow, their voices shaking the world; they further brought incense, flowers, banners, canopies, and music, wailing and weeping piteously as they made offerings to the precious coffin.

At that time, the entire great assembly gathered exquisite fragrant wood, piling it as high as Mount Sumeru; its rich and pervasive fragrance perfumed the entire world. These logs were stacked in dense, overlapping layers to form a great incense pavilion, adorned on all four sides with the seven treasures. Banners, parasols, pennants, flowers, necklaces, and variegated silks filled the sky like clouds, serving as ornaments, while humans and devas offered music and sorrowful worship.

At that time, as the great assembly of devas and humans was about to lift the coffin and place it upon the incense tower, they were overcome once more with profound sorrow; beating their breasts and crying out, their voices shook the great trichiliocosm.
Furthermore, they held up banners, canopies, incense, flowers, and music, making offerings with profound sorrow.

At that time, the great assembly was filled with mournful grief and deep reverence; each covered their hands with white cotton cloth and together lifted the precious reliquary casket of the Great Sage Tathāgata, placing it upon a magnificently adorned and fragrant pavilion. They wailed loudly again, fainting and then reviving, crying out:
"Alas! How bitter!"
"Alas! How could I have expected to be orphaned and exposed, with no one to rely upon?
Weeping with a choked voice, he further scattered fragrant flowers, precious banners, canopies, music, and various silks, offering them with all his heart in sorrowful devotion.

At that time, once the Tathāgata’s great and holy precious coffin had been placed upon the exquisite and subtle precious incense tower, and was about to be set ablaze for the cremation of the Tathāgata, the great assembly again wailed and wept loudly, causing the great trichiliocosm to tremble.
They were once more filled with profound and heavy sorrow as they made offerings to the great and holy precious coffin and the exquisite incense tower.

At that time, the entire great assembly wept with tears filling their eyes; each held a seven-jeweled incense candle as large as a chariot wheel, its radiant flames and variegated light illuminating the entire world.
At that time, they wept bitterly as the cremation pyre was lit, their lamentations shaking the entire trichiliocosm; they further made offerings by filling the area with incense and flowers.
At that moment, the precious torches at the site of the pyre spontaneously went out.

At that time, all the devas again held supreme great torches of the seven jewels whose blazing light shone everywhere; weeping with sorrow, they cast them toward the fragrant tower, yet they were all completely extinguished.
At that time, all the sea deities took great seven-jeweled torches of the fire of the ocean, with countless flames, and threw them into the fragrant tower; yet they too were all extinguished.

At that time, the great assembly wept for a long duration and made every kind of offering; yet they did not know for what reason the Tathāgata had not finished his work when he cast himself into the fragrant tower, and the cremation fire would not ignite.
At that time, the World-Honored One’s great compassion moistened all universally; he waited until the assembly of Kāśyapa arrived before igniting the fire.
At that moment, Mahākāśyapa and his five hundred disciples were on Vulture Peak Mountain, fifty yojanas from the city of Kuśinagara, their bodies and minds tranquil as they entered into samādhi.

While in meditative absorption, his mind was suddenly startled and his entire body trembled; emerging from concentration, he saw that the mountains and earth were all shaking violently, and he immediately knew that the Tathāgata had already entered parinirvāṇa.
He addressed his disciples:
"Our Great Teacher, the Buddha, has entered Parinirvāṇa; seven days have passed since he was placed within the coffin.
Alas! How bitter!"
Alas! We should go swiftly to the place where the Tathāgata is.
I fear he has already entered parinirvāṇa by cremation, and we shall not be able to behold the Buddha’s body of true purity, endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics.

Out of reverence for the Buddha, Kāśyapa did not dare to fly through the air to the Tathāgata’s location; instead, he took his disciples and traveled swiftly along the road, proceeding with sorrowful haste. Exactly seven days later, they arrived at the eastern entrance of the city of Kuśinagara.
Kāśyapa encountered a brahmin carrying a celestial flower who was coming along the road.
Kāśyapa asked him,
"Venerable sir, where are you coming from?"
He replied, "The Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa; I have come from the place of his cremation.
He asked again:
“What flower is this? He replied,
“This celestial flower was obtained from the cremation.”
Kāśyapa went to beg [the bowl], and he replied, "I cannot give it;
I have planned to take it home to show it to my six relations and for their offerings.

Kāśyapa then borrowed it and placed it upon his head; immediately, he fell into a stupor, lost consciousness and collapsed to the ground, choking with sobs and stifled by grief, only reviving after a long while.
He then reflected to himself:
"If I continue to wail here and fail to behold the Tathāgata’s body of purple-gold hue endowed with the eighty minor marks, what benefit will there be in my pursuit?
He immediately advanced quickly with his disciples, reached the northern gate of Kuśinagara, and entered.
Within that city, he entered a monastery and saw various bhikṣus gathered together in one place; he spoke to Kāśyapa, saying, "You have come from afar;
have you not been greatly fatigued?"
“Sit down and wait for the food.
Kāśyapa replied, “My Great Master has already entered nirvāṇa; what feeling could I have to sit here and wait for food?”
The bhikṣus asked,
"Who is your teacher? He replied:
"Do you not know? Alas, what suffering!
The Greatly Awakened World-Honored One has now entered parinirvāṇa."
Having heard this, the bhikṣus were each greatly delighted and spoke these words:
"How wonderful! How wonderful!"
"While the Tathāgata was in the world, he restrained us with severe and rigorous precepts; we found them utterly unbearable and were unable to practice according to them.
Now that he has entered parinirvāṇa, these strict prohibitions and precepts should rightfully be relinquished."
“Wait for your meal; what is so urgent?

By the Buddha’s supernatural power, the ears of all the devas and the disciples of Mahākāśyapa were covered so that they heard nothing of the wicked bhikṣu’s words, except for Mahākāśyapa alone who heard them.
Thereupon, Kāśyapa, with his disciples weeping and shedding tears, hurried to the place where the Buddha was.
At that time, Kāśyapa and his disciples thought to themselves in secret:
"How may we obtain various offerings to bring to the Buddha's presence and present as an offering to the Tathāgata?"
Kāśyapa spoke again:
"I have lived and grown up in this city; it should be possible for me to obtain offerings through begging.

Taking his disciples, he immediately went into the city and begged from door to door. He obtained a full thousand pieces of exquisite white cotton cloth, as well as countless fine tūla-cotton, and immeasurable quantities of precious flowers, fragrant mud, scented water, scented oil, jeweled banners, pennants, canopies, music, stringed songs, necklaces, and various colored silks—all were fully provided.
Kāśyapa and his disciples, weeping with grief, immediately set out in haste toward the western gate of the city.
At that time, Kāśyapa heard the entire great assembly at the site of the cremation wailing and sobbing with choked voices as they asked Śakra Devendra:
"The offerings have already been completed; how may fire be obtained to ignite this fragrant tower and cremate the Tathāgata?"
Śakra replied, "Wait a moment, O assembly; Mahākāśyapa will arrive immediately.

Before he had finished speaking, while the entire great assembly was still in the midst of their lamentation, they suddenly saw Kāśyapa approaching along the path with his disciples, weeping. The assembly immediately ceased their wailing and made way for him.

Kāśyapa stepped forward and, seeing the Buddha’s coffin from afar, led his disciples in prostrating themselves all at once. Wailing and sobbing, they fainted and fell to the ground; their minds were clouded and disordered. After a long while, they regained consciousness, unable to contain their flowing tears as they gradually moved forward.
Addressing the great assembly, he asked: "How can we open the holy coffin of Great Compassion?"
The great assembly replied, “It has already been two weeks since the Buddha entered nirvana; we fear that the body may have suffered damage.
How can it be opened? Kāśyapa replied:

“The body of the Tathāgata is as firm and solid as a diamond; it is eternal, blissful, self, and pure, incapable of being destroyed. Its fragrance of virtue is as pervasive and exquisite as a mountain of sandalwood.”
Having spoken these words, with tears streaming down his face, he went to the place where the Buddha’s coffin was.

At that time, through the Tathāgata’s great compassion and impartiality, for the sake of Kāśyapa, the coffin opened spontaneously; the thousand layers of white cotton cloth and the tufted silk-wool were all instantly unraveled, revealing the physical body of true gold and polished purple, firm and solid, adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics.

When Kāśyapa and his disciples saw this, they fainted and fell to the ground; choking with sobs and stifled by grief, they regained consciousness only after a long while. With tears filling their eyes, they slowly ascended the incense tower with their disciples and drew near to the side of the Buddha’s coffin.

Once again, he choked with sobs and wailed in bitter grief; he then used the incense, flowers, banners, canopies, jewels, pennants, necklaces, music, and stringed songs he had obtained to offer in lamentation as an act of worship. He washed the golden body of the Tathāgata with fragrant clay and scented water, burning incense and scattering flowers while weeping sorrowfully in devotion.

When the washing was completed, Kāśyapa and his disciples took the exquisite *tūla* cotton they had obtained and wrapped it around the Tathāgata’s body, which was the color of purple-polished gold; next, they wrapped old cotton over the new *tūla*.

Once the *tūla* was wrapped, they further took the one thousand sheets of white woolen cloth they had obtained and wrapped them over the *tūla*, layering them one upon another around the Tathāgata’s body.
After wrapping the white woolen cloth, they again took the old woolen cloth and placed it over the new, wrapping them in successive layers.
The shrouding having been completed, the coffin doors were immediately closed, adorned with all manner of ornaments and necklaces of the seven precious gems.

At that time, Kāśyapa again succumbed to profound grief; together with his disciples, he circumambulated [the coffin] seven times to the right, his eyes brimming with tears. Kneeling long and joining his palms, he spoke this verse in lamentation:
"Alas, alas! O Great Sage and Honored One, My heart is now tormented by bitter poison."
How swift was the Blessed One’s parinirvāṇa; why could his great compassion not wait for me?
While in meditative concentration upon Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, I searched everywhere for the Tathāgata but saw him nowhere;
then, seeing that the Buddha had already entered nirvāṇa, my heart suddenly trembled with great alarm.
Suddenly I saw dark clouds pervading the world, And again beheld the mountains and earth shaking violently;
I knew immediately that the Tathāgata had entered parinirvāṇa, Which is why I hastened here, only to find him no longer present.
The World-Honored One’s great compassion did not extend to me;
It caused me not to witness the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, nor to receive even a single word of instruction. Now that I am orphaned and exposed, upon what shall I rely?
World-Honored One, I am now in great agony; my mind is disordered, bewildered, and clouded.
Shall I now prostrate at the crown of the World-Honored One’s head? Or shall I sorrowfully prostrate at the Tathāgata’s chest?
Or shall I reverently prostrate at the Great Sage’s hands? Or shall I piteously prostrate at the Tathāgata’s waist?
Am I paying homage to the navel of the Tathāgata, or am I, with a profound mind, bowing at the Buddha’s feet?
Why is it that I do not see the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa?
I only pray that you will show me the place where I should pay my respects.
While the Tathāgata was in the world, all were at peace; now that he has entered nirvāṇa, all suffer great pain.
Alas, alas! This is profound and great suffering; may Great Compassion show us where we should pay our respects.

At that time, Kāśyapa, choked with sobs and filled with grief, had finished reciting these verses. Then, the World-Honored One, out of great compassion, manifested the mark of the thousand-spoked wheel on his two feet, emerging from outside the coffin and turning to show it to Kāśyapa. From those thousand spokes, he emitted a thousand rays of light, which illuminated all worlds throughout the ten directions.

At that time, Kāśyapa and his disciples, having beheld the Buddha’s feet, simultaneously prostrated themselves before the mark of the thousand-spoked wheel; they immediately fell into a swoon again, collapsing unconscious to the ground, and only after a long while did they regain consciousness.

Together with his disciples, he wailed and choked with sobs; he circumambulated the Buddha seven times to the right, and having completed the seven circumambulations, he again prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, weeping in such deep sorrow that the sound shook the world.
He further spoke in verse, lamenting for the Buddha’s feet:
“The Tathāgata has perfected the mind of great compassion; With impartial light of loving-kindness, he shines without distinction.
When sentient beings have a resonance with him, none fail to receive his response; He now reveals to me the thousand-spoked wheels upon his two feet.”
With a profound heart, I now take refuge and pay homage to the two venerable feet marked with the thousand-spoked wheel;
from within those thousand-spoked wheels, a thousand rays of light are emitted, universally illuminating the Buddha-fields throughout the ten directions.
I now take refuge and prostrate with my head; The mark of the thousand-spoked wheel radiates long beams of light.
When sentient beings encounter this light, they all attain liberation; Those in the three miserable realms and the eight difficulties are all freed from suffering.
I take refuge once more and prostrate with my head bowed; The light of your wheel universally rescues all from the evil realms.
In the past, throughout countless eons, World-Honored One, You practiced austerities for our sake;
Now you have realized this vajra-body, From beneath which a thousand rays of light are emitted.
With sorrowful reverence, I bow my head and take refuge; The thousand-spoked wheel brings peace to all sentient beings.
The Buddha cultivated myriad virtues for the sake of all; On the day he attained enlightenment at the Bodhi tree, he subdued the four Māras.
Having subdued the four Māras, he overcame the non-Buddhists; By this means, sentient beings attain right view.

I prostrate with my head at his feet in refuge; To the Buddha, whose light-footed rays of right view illuminate all beings, Who is the true father of compassion for all, Whose radiance from his feet equally delivers sentient beings.
I take refuge once more, bowing my head in homage to the light from the soles of the feet that equally liberate from the wheel of suffering;
having encountered these feet with their thousand-spoked radiance, my heart is moved by a profound interplay of sorrow and joy.
I again prostrate with head and face in sorrowful lamentation; Moved by my feeling, there appears the mark of the thousand-spoked wheel light.
I bow my head in refuge to the light of the wheels on your feet, Riding the ultimate vehicle to transcend the triple world.
I pay homage to the one whose feet are the refuge of gods and humans; The light of his wheels universally illuminates the suffering of the three realms of existence.
Until all sentient beings have attained the gateway to liberation from suffering, They shall all take refuge in those feet with their wheel-marks.
We have not yet escaped from saṃsāra; how could you cast off your wheel-marked feet?
Alas, alas for all sentient beings! Throughout the long night they shall not behold the light of your wheel-marked feet.
We repent before the World-Honored One of great compassion, who reveals his reverent feet shining with the light of the thousand-spoked wheel.
"Alas! Having now encountered the mark of the wheel-light, from this point forward, when shall we behold it again?

At that time, after Kāśyapa and his disciples had spoken these verses, they fell into a deep faint once more, collapsing to the ground in a state of unconsciousness. After a long while, they gradually regained consciousness; overcome with grief and sobbing, they were unable to compose themselves.
The Greatly Awakened World-Honored One’s feet, marked with the thousand-spoked wheel and like vajras, returned of their own accord into the coffin, which was then sealed as before.

At that time, all the men and women, devas and humans, and the great assembly within the city saw Mahākāśyapa weeping once more, beating his breast and crying out so loudly that his grief shook the immeasurable worlds of the trichiliocosm; each brought what they held, offering it with choked sobs of sorrow.

At that time, there were four strongmen within the city of Kuśinagara who adorned their bodies with necklaces and held seven-jeweled torches as large as chariot wheels; their blazing light shone everywhere as they used them to cremate the Tathāgata at the incense tower. When the torches were cast onto the incense tower, they were spontaneously extinguished.
Kāśyapa replied, "The precious coffin of the Great Sage cannot be burned even by the fires of the three realms; how much less could it be burned by your strength?
Within the city, there were also eight powerful wrestlers who further took seven-jeweled torches with blazing flames and all cast them toward the coffin, yet they too were completely extinguished.

Within the city, there were furthermore sixteen extremely powerful giants, each holding a great torch made of the seven treasures, who came and threw them onto the fragrant tower, yet they were all utterly extinguished.

Within the city, there were furthermore thirty-six extremely powerful giants, each holding a great torch made of the seven treasures, who came and threw them [onto the tower], yet they too were all utterly extinguished.
At that time, Kāśyapa addressed the Mallas and the entire great assembly:
"You should know that even if all the gods and humans were to gather every torch and fire, they would not be able to cremate the Tathāgata’s precious coffin."
"You need not trouble yourselves to force me to act.

At that time, the men and women within the city, the devas and humans, and the great assembly were once again overcome with grief; each offered worship while wailing and weeping, bowing down and circumambulating him seven times to the right. Their cries of lamentation and loud weeping shook the trichiliocosm.

At that time, by the power of great compassion, flames leaped from the Tathāgata’s chest out of the coffin and gradually cremated him; after seven days had passed, the cremation of the Pavilion of Exquisite Incense was finally completed.

At that time, for seven days, the men and women, devas and humans, and the great assembly within the city wailed and wept with unceasing lamentation; each offered whatever they possessed as an act of worship without ceasing.
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings each had this thought:
"I shall pour scented water upon the fire to extinguish it, and quickly collect the relics to offer them in the heavens."

Having formed this thought, he immediately took seven-jeweled golden vases filled with fragrant water, and further brought from the four peaks of Mount Sumeru four great, pure trees that exude sweet milk; each tree was a thousand fathoms in circumference and a hundred yojanas in height, descending simultaneously with the Four Heavenly Kings to the site of the cremation.
The trees flowed with sweet milk, which poured into incense jars; all at once, they were poured onto the fire.
Once poured, the flames rose even higher and could not be extinguished at all.
At that time, the ocean deity Sāgara, the Dragon King, along with the deities of the rivers and streams, seeing that the fire would not be extinguished, each had this thought:
"I shall take fragrant water and pour it over the fire to extinguish it, then quickly collect the relics to enshrine and worship them at my dwelling place.
Having formed this thought, each of them took a precious vessel filled with immeasurable fragrant water and went to the site of the cremation, pouring the water onto the fire all at once.
After he had poured it out, the intensity of the flames remained as before and was not extinguished at all.
At that time, Loutou said to the Four Heavenly Kings, the Sea God, and the others:
"If you pour scented water and cause the fire to be extinguished, would you not wish to take the śarīra and return to your own abodes to make offerings to them?"
He replied, "It is indeed so. Then,
Rudrāyaṇa spoke to the Four Heavenly Kings:
"You have a great greedy mind.
You dwell in the heavens, yet the śarīra follows you; if it remains in a celestial palace, how can those who dwell on earth go there to make offerings?"
He spoke again to the sea deities:
"Since you dwell within the great oceans and rivers, how can those who live upon the earth go there to receive and make offerings to the Tathāgata’s relics that you have taken up?"
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings all immediately repented; having repented, they each returned to their celestial palaces.
At that time, the deities of the great oceans, rivers, and streams likewise all repented, saying, "It is truly as the Holy One has spoken," and having repented, they each returned.

Chapter Four: The Vast and Moisture-Infused Holy Body. *The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, Chapter Four: The Vast and Moisture-Infused Holy Body. At that time, Śakra, holding a vessel of the seven precious gems and various articles of offering, arrived at the site of the cremation. The fire was then spontaneously extinguished all at once. Śakra immediately opened the Tathāgata’s precious coffin, wishing to request the Buddha’s tooth relic.
Loudou immediately asked,
"What are you doing? He replied:
"I wish to request the Buddha’s tooth relic to take back to the heavens for veneration. Loutou said:
"Do not take it yourself haphazardly; you should wait for the great assembly, and only then share it together."
Śakra said, "The Buddha previously gave me one tooth-relic; it was for this reason that I came, and thus the fire extinguished itself.

After Śakra had spoken these words, he opened the precious coffin and took the tooth-relic from the upper right jaw inside the Buddha's mouth. He then returned to the heavens to erect a stupa and make offerings to it.
At that time, there were two swift rākṣasas who followed the assembly while concealing their bodies so that no one could see them; they stole a pair of the Buddha’s tooth-relics.
Thereupon, all the men and women within the city, along with the entire multitude, came at once, desiring to contend for the relics.
Loudou addressed them, saying:
"Venerable assembly, you should know: wait and remain composed.
As the Buddha has taught, you should divide the offerings equally according to the Dharma."

At that time, the men and women within the city and the entire multitude, not hearing what Loutou had said, each took up spears, javelins, bows and arrows, swords, lassos, and all manner of weapons of war; having adorned themselves individually, they desired to take the śarīra.

At that time, the multitude within the city opened the Buddha’s coffin; the cotton wool and white fine cloth remained perfectly unburnt. Upon seeing this, the great assembly wailed even more bitterly, their tears filling their eyes. Each took what they held as an offering of sorrow, prostrating with deep devotion. Weeping, they knelt for a long time and together spoke these verses of praise:
"By the power of Great Sovereignty, the Tathāgata has attained mastery over all worlds.
Through the original vow of Great Compassion, he dwells in this land, circling through the sea of suffering to deliver sentient beings."
With immeasurable wisdom and the power of spiritual penetrations, they appear and disappear within birth and death without hindrance;
they can manifest a single body as many bodies, and many bodies as a single body, extending to the infinite.
His divine transformations respond universally so that all may see; yet when there are no conditions, he immediately manifests entry into nirvana.
Our merit is exhausted and we lack the conditions for his response; therefore, the Tathāgata has now forsaken us.
Within the precious sarira-encasement of the śāla trees, the Great Strongmen could not lift it;
by the power of his great compassion, he himself lifted it lightly, ascending into the air to the height of a tāla tree.
Traveling through space, he slowly circumambulated the city of Kuśinagara; for seven days, the Great Sage performed seven circuits.
Having circumambulated, he personally approached the site of the cremation; this was an act performed through shared supernatural power.
None among all devas and humans could fathom it: within the Great Parinirvāṇa, the Buddha possessed the sovereign power of indestructible adamant; thus, none of the cremation fires would ignite.
From within his own heart he brought forth the fire of loving-kindness, Which burned for seven days until it appeared to be extinguished;
Neither humans nor devas could extinguish this fire— Such is the power of the Tathāgata’s great compassion manifesting through skillful means.
When Śakra arrived, the fire was instantly extinguished; The Buddha’s body was wrapped in exquisite tūla-cotton, yet the great flames could not burn it at all.
The white cotton cloth followed the Buddha into the precious coffin;
Within the fire, it remained solemnly unburnt. Only then did they realize the Tathāgata’s power of mastery.
Sovereign over the Dharma, King of the Dharma—homage to you, the Great Compassionate One, Honored One of the Three Realms;
homage to the Sage among those who are fearless; homage to the one of great compassionate power who universally covers all;
homage to the one with mastery over miraculous transformations. From this day forth, we are separated from the World-Honored One.
Immersed in suffering, none can see to rescue or protect us.
Alas, alas, Great Holy One!
Now that we must part forever, by what means shall we see you again?
At that time, after the great assembly had spoken these verses, they wept once more with grief, each offering what they held as a final act of mourning and veneration.
Then, for the sake of the devas, humans, and the entire great assembly, together with the people of the city, Rudrāyaṇa slowly lifted the white cotton cloth and the *tūla* cotton from the coffin;
the thousand sheets of white cotton belonging to Kāśyapa and the others were entirely unburned by the fire.
Within that city, of the thousand pieces of fine white cotton cloth, with the exception of one outer layer, the rest were reduced to ashes;
however, the *tūla* cotton remained exactly as it was before.

At that time, Loutou took this white cotton cloth and the *tūla* cotton, tore them into small pieces, and distributed them to the great assembly, instructing them to erect jeweled stupas to make offerings to them.
Loudou again took the cotton ash and divided it among the assembly once more, instructing them to erect jeweled stupas as offerings;
as for the remaining ashes, there was no further portion to divide, so each member of the assembly took some for themselves and erected stupas to make offerings.

The people within that city had previously sent artisans to construct eight golden jars and eight lion thrones, each adorned with the seven precious gems; these seven-jeweled jars, each with a capacity of one *hu*, were placed upon the seven-jeweled lion thrones.

Each of those eight lion thrones made of the seven treasures was supported by thirty-two powerful men, each adorned with the seven treasures, necklaces, and various colored cloths wrapped around their bodies, together lifting the eight lion thrones of the seven treasures.
Upon each throne were likewise eight court ladies, their bodies adorned with the seven treasures, necklaces, and various colored cloths, holding jars of the seven treasures;
upon each throne were furthermore eight court ladies, their bodies adorned with necklaces, holding canopies of the seven treasures to cover the golden jars.
Upon each seat were further eight court ladies, their bodies adorned with necklaces and ornaments, holding swords of the seven treasures to guard the urns of the seven treasures;
upon each seat were further eight court ladies, their bodies adorned with necklaces and ornaments, holding peacock-feather banners to stand at the four sides of the urns.
Separately for each seat, there were immeasurable multitudes of people, holding exquisite music, banners, streamers, precious parasols, fragrant flowers, and necklaces, surrounding them in worship.

On each seat there were also immeasurable multitudes of people, each holding bows and arrows, spears and lances, nooses, long hooks, and all manner of weapons of war, surrounding him as they followed from the city of Kuśinagara, encircling him before and behind, toward the place of cremation.

After the eight lion thrones made of the seven precious gems had departed from the city, the multitude within the city immediately took countless fragrant muds and scented waters. Following behind the Mallas, they leveled and smeared the ground, creating a fragrant mud road that was vast and magnificently adorned, leading toward the place of cremation.

On both sides of the road, countless jeweled banners, canopies, incense, flowers, pearls, necklaces, various exquisite multicolored silks, music, and stringed songs adorned the roadside; they stood solemnly as offerings, awaiting the return of the Great Holy One’s relics.

The various Mallas, carrying the eight-lion throne made of the seven treasures, surrounded it and proceeded to the site of the cremation; there they wept with great sorrow, wailing and sobbing until their voices shook the great trichiliocosm, each making offerings with profound sincerity according to what they held.

At that time, by the power of the World-Honored One’s great compassion, his adamantine body was crushed into powdered relics (*śarīra*), with the exception of four teeth which remained indestructible.
When the great assembly saw these relics, they were once again overcome with grief and offered them their tears from the vessels they held.

At that time, Loutou and the people within the city wept until their eyes were filled with tears; they gathered the śarīra relics and placed them in a casket of seven precious gems upon the lion throne, filling eight golden urns until the relics were exhausted.

At that time, the entire assembly of devas and humans, seeing the Buddha’s śarīra enter the golden urn, wept once more with profound sorrow; shedding tears and streaming with sobs, each offered deep-seated devotion with whatever they held in their hands.
At that time, the great strongmen and the men and women within the city were about to take the golden casket containing the Buddha’s relics toward the city of Kuśinagara.
Then the great assembly again felt profound sorrow; each took what they held and made offerings while shedding tears.

At that time, the great strongmen within the city, the surrounding multitude, and the people of the city wept with choked sobs; they lifted the eight-lion throne made of the seven precious gems and followed the path of fragrant mud back toward Kuśinagara.
At that time, the great assembly of humans and devas again felt profound sorrow, their voices shaking the world as each took what they held and followed the śarīra, wailing and making offerings.
Once the Tathāgata’s relics had reached the city, they were placed at the crossroads.

At that time, the people of Kuśinagara immediately arrayed the fourfold army and countless troops; donning armor and each grasping weapons of war, they surrounded the city of Kuśinagara on all four sides with countless ranks of solemn soldiers. This was done to prevent outsiders from coming to plunder, yet though it was a formal display of defense, they harbored no intent for combat or strife.
Furthermore, there were five hundred great masters of incantations stationed at the four gates of the city to ward off obstacles.

Additionally, countless jeweled banners, pennants, and canopies, exquisitely adorned with great pheasant-feather streamers, were solemnly offered at the four corners of the city as a mark of distinction.

At that time, all the men and women within the city, as well as the great assembly of devas and humans, were again filled with profound sorrow and each offered deep-seated devotion with whatever they held.

The reliquary casket was placed upon a lion throne for seven days; during these seven days, the entire great assembly wailed day and night, their cries of grief unceasing, as they all made offerings with deep-seated devotion using whatever they possessed.

Each of those eight lion thrones made of the seven precious gems was supported by five hundred great masters of incantations, who held them together to prevent devas, nāgas, yakṣas, spirits, and ghosts from coming to deceive or seize them.

After seven days had passed, at that time, the Tathāgata’s original kinsmen—the King of Kapilavastu, the various Śākyas, and their followers—due to the Buddha’s supernatural power, were entirely unaware that the Buddha had entered parinirvāṇa.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, it was only after twenty-one days had passed that they finally learned of it.

At that time, the king of that country and the various Śākya clansmen wailed and wept in grief; they immediately hurried together to the city of Kuśinagara. There they saw the military forces, numbering many thousands, surrounding the city;
they also saw jeweled banners, streamers, and canopies arrayed at the four quarters of the city, their splendor overshadowing the entire realm.
Furthermore, he saw a great master of incantations guarding the four gates of the city.
The King and the Śākyas asked the master of incantations:
"Has the Buddha entered nirvāṇa?"
He replied, "Since the Buddha entered nirvana, more than four weeks have passed; the cremation has been completed, and the śarīras are about to be divided.
The King said:
"We are the kinsmen born of the Buddha; it is by the Buddha’s spiritual power that we were made unaware of the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa.
We now wish to see the relics of the Tathāgata; you should clear a path so that we may enter."
Upon hearing these words, the sorcerer and his troops immediately granted them entry into the city.

Once the King and the Śākyas had entered the city, they beheld the Buddha’s relics upon the lion throne; overcome with grief, they wailed and choked with emotion, their tears flowing profusely as they circumambulated it seven times to the right.
Having circumambulated [the stupa] seven times, he wiped away his tears and said,
"I now wish to request one portion of the Tathāgata’s relics to take back and offer them in worship.
The great assembly replied:

"Although we know you are a kinsman of the Śākya clan, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has already stated that when the śarīra were distributed, they did not reach you; each portion had its own patron, so how could you have obtained any?"
"May you return.

At that time, the king and the Śākyas, their requests unfulfilled, wailed and lamented in grief; they fainted and fell to the ground, regaining consciousness only after a long while. Overcome by sorrow beyond measure, they spoke to the multitude, saying:
"The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, was of our Śākya clan; out of compassion for you all, he has entered nirvana here."
"How is it that you all see fit to treat us with such contempt as to refuse to grant us even a single portion of the śarīra?

Having spoken these words, they each paid homage to the śarīra, circumambulated it seven times to the right, and weeping with tears streaming down, they returned home filled with resentment and grief.

At that time, King Ajātaśatru, the ruler of Magadha, having murdered his father the king, was deeply overcome with remorse. A malignant ulcer broke out upon his body; however, when he encountered the World-Honored One, the moon-like light of the Buddha’s radiance touched his sores, which gradually healed. He then came to the Buddha’s dwelling to seek refuge and repent.

The World-Honored One, out of great compassion, immediately washed away the sores upon his body with the subtle medicinal elixir of the Dharma; his most grievous offenses were extinguished, and he returned to his original palace, remaining entirely unaware that the Tathāgata had entered parinirvāṇa.
On the night of his parinirvāṇa, he dreamed that the moon fell, the sun rose from the earth, and the constellations, clouds, and rain descended in profusion;
furthermore, smoke issued forth from the ground, and he saw seven comets appear in the heavens;
moreover, he dreamed of a great mass of fire in the sky, blazing throughout the void, which all at once fell to the earth.
Having awakened from the dream, his heart was greatly startled and trembling; he immediately summoned his ministers and related this dream in detail, asking:
"What omen is this?
The ministers replied to the king:
"This is an inauspicious omen of the Buddha’s *nirvāṇa*.

After the Buddha has passed into extinction, the sentient beings of the three realms and the conscious beings of the six paths will give rise to afflictions (*kleśa*) in profusion; therefore, a great fire appears, falling from the heavens to the earth.

As the Buddha enters *parinirvāṇa*, the moon-like compassionate light and the wisdom-clouds that universally moisten all things are entirely extinguished and vanish; this is why the clouds and the moon have fallen."

The falling of the stars signifies that after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, eighty thousand rules of discipline and all the precepts will be violated by sentient beings; no longer relying on the Buddha's teachings, they will instead practice false dharmas and fall into the hells.
The rising of the sun from the earth signifies that after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the sunlight of the mass of suffering in the three miserable realms and evil paths will appear in the world;
thus was this dream experienced.

Upon hearing these words, the king, accompanied by his ministers and retinue, arrived at the city of Kuśinagara at midnight. He saw countless hosts of the fourfold army guarding Kuśinagara in immeasurable layers, and he further saw incantation masters at the city gates warding off external threats.
Having seen this, the king immediately asked the mantra-master:
"Has the Buddha entered nirvana?
The mantra-master replied:
“It has been twenty-eight years since the Buddha entered nirvana, and now the great assembly is about to divide the śarīra.

The King said, “I was entirely unaware that the Buddha had entered nirvana; it was only when I saw an inauspicious omen in a dream last night and questioned my ministers that I learned the Tathāgata had entered Great Nirvana.”
"I wish to enter the city to pay homage to the Tathāgata’s diamond-like *śarīra*; you must clear a path for me.
Upon hearing this, the mantra-master immediately permitted him to proceed.

When the king reached the crossroads within the city, he beheld the lion throne and the golden casket containing the *śarīra*. He further observed the great assembly making offerings with deep sorrow; the king and his retinue simultaneously prostrated themselves, weeping with tears streaming down their faces, circumambulating it seven times to the right while making offerings with profound grief.
At that time, the king approached the great assembly and requested one portion of the Tathāgata’s relics to take back to his kingdom for veneration.
The assembly replied,
"Why have you arrived so late?"

The Buddha had already previously explained the method for distributing [the relics], and all the śarīras had already been requested by various parties; there was no portion remaining for you, so you may return to your palace.
King Ajātaśatru, his request having failed, was filled with grief and distress; he then paid homage to the śarīras and returned in dejection.

At that time, there was a non-Buddhist king named Vaira who, only after three weeks had passed since the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, finally learned of it; he then immediately set out with his ministers and attendants in haste for Kuśinagara.
Upon arriving at Kuśinagara, he immediately saw countless fourfold armies guarding the city in infinite concentric circles.
At that time, King Allakappa learned of the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa only after three weeks had passed; he then promptly set out for Kuśinagara with his ministers and retinue.
Having arrived at Kuśinagara, he immediately saw countless fourfold armies guarding Kuśinagara in infinite layers of encirclement.
At that time, King Virūḍhaka did not realize it until three weeks had passed since the Buddha entered nirvāṇa.
At that time, the King of Cālikā and Kālika only learned of it after the Buddha had entered nirvana for three weeks.
At that time, King Śreṇika only learned of it after the Buddha had entered nirvana for three weeks.

At that time, the non-Buddhist king named Prasenajit learned of the Buddha’s entry into nirvana only after three weeks had passed; he immediately set out for Kuśinagara with his ministers and retinue in haste.
Having arrived at Kuśinagara, he immediately saw countless fourfold armies guarding Kuśinagara in infinite layers of encirclement.
He further saw great incantation masters at the city gates warding off external threats. The king asked the incantation masters, "Has the Buddha entered nirvāṇa?"
He replied, "Since the Buddha entered parinirvāṇa, four weeks have already passed; the great assembly is now about to divide the śarīra.
The king said to the mantra-master:
“I was entirely unaware that the Buddha had entered parinirvāṇa, which is why I have arrived so late this evening.
I wish to enter the city to pay homage and make offerings to the Tathāgata’s relics; you should clear a path for me.”
Upon hearing this, the mantra-master immediately granted him permission to enter.

Arriving at the crossroads, he saw a lion throne adorned with the seven precious gems, upon which was placed a golden casket containing the relics of the seven precious substances. He further beheld the great assembly making offerings with deep sorrow; the king and his retinue simultaneously prostrated themselves, weeping with grief, circumambulated the throne seven times to the right, and each made their own offerings with profound lamentation.
The king said to the assembly:
"I was entirely unaware that the Buddha had entered nirvana; how bitter it is that I have not been able to see him!
I beg you all to grant me a portion of the śarīra so that I may return to my kingdom and make offerings."
The assembly said:

"Why have you arrived so late? The Buddha has already previously explained the ritual procedures for the distribution of the relics, and all the śarīras have already been requested by others; there is no portion remaining for you. You may return to your palace."
The king and his assembly of ministers, their requests having been denied, were filled with sorrow and distress; they paid homage to the śarīra and returned home in grief and longing.

At that time, the assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas, devas, humans, nāgas, yakṣas, kings, elders, ministers, commoners, and all the great multitude wailed and wept, beating their breasts and crying out loudly; prostrating themselves with their five limbs touching the ground, they paid their respects and departed.

In the lower fascicle of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, at that time, the seven kings and their ministers, such as Kāpilavastu, having failed to achieve their wishes, returned home with hearts filled with grief and indignation. Lamenting their loss, they each arrived at their own capitals and dispatched envoys together to Kuśinagara to once again seek the śarīra.

The city-dwellers replied, "Since the World-Honored One, our compassionate father, has entered parinirvāṇa within our realm, his entire body of relics (śarīra) should remain here for eternal kalpas to be venerated; we shall by no means share them with the people of other towns."
The various kingdoms replied:
"If you divide it, that would be well;
if you do not give it to us, we shall seize it by force."
The city-dwellers replied,
"Engaging in mere strife will ultimately yield nothing.
King Ajātaśatru again dispatched the minister Vṛṣṭika with troops to request a division of the territory, saying to the city-dwellers:
"If you give it to me, that would be well;
if you do not grant me a share, I shall employ military force to seize it by violence and take it away.
He replied:
"According to your pleasure.
At that time, all the men and women who were warriors within the city of Kuśinagara were skilled in archery;
they immediately came forth together, arrayed the fourfold army, and desired to engage in battle with the various settlements.
At that time, the Licchavis of Vaiśālī assembled their fourfold army and went to the city of Kuśinagara, where they stationed themselves to one side;
the Kṣatriyas of Allakappa also assembled their fourfold army and stationed themselves to one side;
and the Brahmins of Viṇḍa also assembled their fourfold army and stationed themselves to one side.
The Śākyas of the kingdom of Calakalpa also assembled their fourfold army and stood to one side;
the Kauravas of the kingdom of Sīkā also assembled their fourfold army and stood to one side;
and the Mallas of the kingdom of Pāpā also assembled their fourfold army and went to the city of Kuśinagara, standing to one side.
At that time, the city of Kuśinagara was surrounded by seven armies, each desiring to seize the śarīras for their own sake.
Then, among the great assembly, there was a brahmin of the Vāsiṣṭha clan who, amidst the eight armies, cried out in a loud voice:
"Listen, O leaders of the Mallas of Kuśinagara! The Buddha accumulated merit and practiced patience through immeasurable kalpas; you all have also constantly heard this."
Praising the Dharma of patience, how can you today, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, raise armies to seize one another for the sake of relics?
You gentlemen should know that this is not an act of reverence.
"The Śarīra should now simply be divided into eight portions.
The Mallas said, "We respectfully accept the Tathāgata’s proposal."
At that time, the brahmin Dhūma divided the śarīra into eight portions. Having completed the division into eight parts, he cried out in a loud voice:

"Listen, you leaders of the Mallas! Please grant me the urn that contained the śarīra; I wish to return to the village of Pippalivana to erect an urn-stūpa and offer flowers, incense, banners, canopies, and music in worship."
The Mallas replied,
"We respectfully accept your invitation.
At that time, the Brahmin and householder Pippalāyana again shouted out at the top of his voice:

"Listen, O leaders of the Mallas in the city of Kuśinagara! Give me the charcoal from the place where the Buddha was cremated; I wish to return to my own country to erect a charnel-relic stupa and offer it worship with flowers, incense, and music."
The Mallas replied to the brahmin, saying,
"We respectfully accept your invitation."
At that time, the Mallas of Kuśinagara obtained the first portion of the relics; they immediately erected a stūpa within their city and made various offerings of flowers, incense, and music.
The Mallas of Pāpā obtained the second portion of the relics; they returned home and erected a stūpa, making various offerings.
The Koliyas of Rāmagrāma obtained the third portion of the relics; they returned home and erected a stūpa, making various offerings.
The Kṣatriyas of the country of Allakappa obtained the fourth portion of the relics; they returned to their country, erected a stūpa, and made offerings.
The Brahmins of the country of Veṇugrāma obtained the fifth portion of the relics; they returned to their country, erected a stūpa, and made various kinds of offerings.
The Licchavis of the country of Vaiśālī obtained the sixth portion of the relics; they returned to their country, erected a stūpa, and made various kinds of offerings.
The Śākyas of the kingdom of Cālakalpa obtained the seventh portion of the relics; they returned to their country, erected a stūpa, and made offerings of flowers and incense.
Ajātaśatru, the King of Magadha, obtained the eighth portion of the relics;
he returned to the city of Rājagṛha, erected a stūpa, and made various offerings of flowers, incense, music, and dance.
The brahmin named Agni obtained a full relic jar and returned to the village of Thūna, where he erected a stūpa and made offerings of flowers and incense;
the brahmin and householder Vepacitti obtained the charcoal and returned to his kingdom, where he erected a stūpa and made offerings.
At that time, the distribution of the relics throughout Jambudvīpa was completed, consisting of eight relic stupas, a ninth flask stupa, and a tenth charcoal stupa.
